G3632.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds an important truth: conversion frees from the bondage to passions. Drunkenness symbolizes the slavery of unbridled desire; by leaving it behind, the believer experiences the new freedom that Christ gives. This passage also invites us to examine our own habits and ask ourselves if we honor our bodies, which are the temple of the Holy Spirit.

sens: To suppose or believe something probable
To imagine, to represent something
To estimate, to hold an opinion on something
G3633.detail:
1. To think primarily expresses the idea of supposing, of believing probable. The verb implies a certain uncertainty: it is not a firm assertion, but an opinion, a conjecture. In John 21:25, John writes: "I do not think that the world itself could contain the books" — he supposes, estimates it probable that the whole world would not suffice.

2. To think can also mean to imagine or to picture a situation. It is to mentally represent something that is not immediately visible. This is the figurative sense of the supposed: to create a mental image.

3. Finally, the verb can mean to estimate or judge a thing in a certain way. In James 1:7, the one who doubts should not "imagine" he will receive anything from the Lord: it is a mistaken conviction about what one can expect.
G3633.origine: The Greek verb οἴομαι (oiomaï) is a deponent verb in ancient Greek (it has a passive form but an active meaning). It belongs to the family of verbs expressing opinion and judgment. The Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) sometimes used it to translate the Hebrew הִנֵּה (hinné), "behold," but this link is not constant. The word belongs to the group of verbs meaning "to think," "to believe," "to suppose," with others like ἡγέομαι (hegeomaï, "to lead," "to estimate").
G3633.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament according to the documented usages. In John 21:25, John uses it to express a reserved opinion: he does not believe it possible that the books containing all that Jesus has done could fit in the world. It is a humbly stated supposition. In James 1:7, the context is that of prayer and faith: the man who prays without conviction should not imagine or suppose that he will receive anything from the Lord. In both cases, the verb marks an opinion subordinate to objective reality.
G3633.portee: This verb invites the reader to distinguish between supposing and knowing, between imagining and truly believing. In John 21:25, it is humble: the work of Jesus exceeds all measure. In James 1:7, it warns: it is not enough to mentally picture that one will receive from God; true faith is required. The word reminds us that personal opinion and imagination never replace the reality of faith in God.

sens: Of what sort, of what nature (interrogative or indefinite)
Such, of this sort (without a correlating 'thus')
Expressing a comparison or equivalence between two realities
G3634.detail:
1. The word asks: "What kind? Of what sort?" It serves to qualify something whose exact nature is unknown or to emphasize its intensity. In Matthew 24:21, Jesus speaks of a distress "such as has not been seen before": he does not precisely describe the distress, but emphasizes its unprecedented character.
2. It simply states: "It is such, it is so." Without making a comparison with a correlating word (like "thus"), it affirms a quality or nature. In Romans 9:6, Paul says, "It is not to say that the word of God has failed": the word translated here as "this" does not pose a question but establishes a fact of a particular nature.
3. It brings two things together to show that they are of the same kind or have the same character. In 2 Corinthians 10:11, Paul asserts: "Such we are in words in our letters, so we are in our actions" — the same word expresses that his actions correspond to his words, that there is a coherence of nature between the two.
G3634.origine: The Greek word comes from an ancient interrogative root that asks "what? of what sort?" It is related to the relative pronoun "who" (ὅς), just as the Latin "qualis" (of what sort) is related to "who." In Hebrew, this meaning often corresponds to interrogative words like "mi" or to comparative phrases. The form captures the idea of an inquiry into the nature or character of a thing.
G3634.emploi: The word appears 12 times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul and in Revelation. It is primarily used to emphasize intensity or the absence of precedent: Matthew 24:21 and Mark 13:19 speak of a distress "such" that none has ever equaled. It then expresses an equivalence between two states: in 2 Corinthians 10:11, Paul unites his actions and his words with the same adjective to show that they are of the same order. Romans 9:6 uses it to introduce a correction: "it is not to say that...", where the word marks the error to avoid. Revelation 16:18 uses it to qualify an earthquake "such" that there has never been one like it.
G3634.portee: This word teaches the reader to properly qualify things according to their true nature. When the Bible says that the distress of the last days will be "such" that none has preceded it, it orders the believer's thought: he understands that the intensity surpasses any known comparison. In Paul, this word also invites authenticity: one must be "such" in actions as in words, in accordance with one's own nature.

sens: To hesitate, to recoil from an action
To postpone, to defer, to put off until later
G3635.detail:
1. To hesitate, to recoil from an action: this verb primarily expresses the idea of recoiling, fearing to do something, as if feeling a reluctance or fear to act. It is the hesitation that paralyzes action.
2. To delay, to defer, to put off until later: by extension, to delay also means to push something back in time, to postpone it. In Acts 9:38, the disciples ask Peter to come "without delay", meaning without delay, immediately.
G3635.origine: The word comes from the Greek noun ὄκνος (oknos), which means "reluctance, hesitation, fear". The root expresses the idea of recoiling from an effort or difficulty. The verb ὀκνέω describes the action of one who hesitates or drags their feet.
G3635.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 9:38. The disciples of Joppa send two men to pray for Peter to come without delay to them, for Dorcas has just died. The use of the verb in the infinitive with negation ("without delay") shows the urgency of the situation and the importance of the request. The word emphasizes the idea of delay and hesitation that must be avoided in this crisis context.
G3635.portee: This word reminds the Christian that in the face of others' needs, hesitation and delay can be harmful. The example of Peter being invited to come without delay confronts us with our own tendency to postpone what should be done quickly, especially when it comes to serving or helping. To delay can mean missing an opportunity to witness the love of Christ.

sens: Who recoils from effort, who hesitates to act
Who lacks zeal and fervor in work
Who causes fatigue, who tires
G3636.detail:
1. The word first describes an inner attitude: it is the tendency to recoil, to hesitate when one should act. This is perfectly embodied by the servant in Matthew 25:26 — he knew what his master expected of him, but he preferred not to risk anything rather than to exert himself.

2. By extension, it designates one who lacks zeal and fervor: it is lazy inactivity, the absence of sustained effort in work or service. This is why Paul exhorts in Romans 12:11 to be zealous rather than lazy — he calls for an active engagement of the heart and hands.

3. The word can also qualify an action or situation that causes weariness, that tires the one who deals with it. When Paul says in Philippians 3:1 that he does not "grow weary", it is because he does not find it irksome to repeat the same important truths: his love for his brothers surpasses all fatigue.
G3636.origine: The word comes from the verb ὀκνέω which means "to hesitate, to recoil, to fear effort". This root expresses the idea of something that is repugnant, that provokes an inner resistance. In Hebrew and Aramaic of the Old Testament, similar words designate laziness and inactivity as a form of moral cowardice. The family of the word encompasses the entire attitude of one who prefers inaction to risk.
G3636.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, always in contexts of moral exhortation. In Matthew 25:26, it qualifies the unfaithful servant who did not make his talent fruitful: it is laziness as a lack of courage and faithfulness. In Romans 12:11, it designates the attitude opposed to Christian zeal: Paul contrasts laziness with spiritual fervor and commitment to the Lord's service. In Philippians 3:1, the word takes on a slightly different shade: it is no longer a blame, but the absence of weariness despite repetition — Paul does not find the burden heavy. The use thus varies from the negative (the vice to flee) to the positive (the absence of fatigue in good).
G3636.portee: For the Christian, this word reveals the spiritual danger of laziness, not as mere forgetfulness or carnal fatigue, but as an attitude of the heart that recoils from God's call. It opposes the zeal, fervor, and faithfulness that the Lord demands. It is a call not to be satisfied with a lukewarm faith or a half-hearted service, but to seek that fervor of spirit that characterizes the true disciple.

sens: the day that immediately follows the seventh day, or an age of eight days
character of that which lasts eight days or is completed on the eighth day
G3637.detail:
1. The word simply designates the eighth day, the one that comes after the first seven days. In Philippians 3:5, Paul speaks of his circumcision "on the eighth day": this is the time prescribed by the Law to circumcise a male Jewish child, eight days after his birth (see Leviticus 12:3). This period also marked an important religious fulfillment: circumcision on the eighth day demonstrated faithful observance of the Law.
2. The word can also mean "lasting eight days" or "which lasts eight days." It serves to express age or duration: a newborn circumcised "on the eighth day" is literally "eight days old." Paul uses this term to emphasize his grounding in the most scrupulous Jewish traditions.
G3637.origine: The word is composed of two Greek elements: "okta" (eight) and "hémera" (day). It is an adjective that combines these two ideas to form a precise expression of time. Greek would use terms of this type to indicate periods or key moments: "tetartaios" (of the fourth day) functions in the same way. This form reflects the importance that Jewish Law places on the eighth day as a moment of religious consecration.
G3637.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Philippians 3:5. Paul uses it to list his credentials according to the flesh: he presents himself as "circumcised on the eighth day." This mention is part of a passage where the apostle recaps all his impeccable Jewish qualifications — his race, his tribe, his sect, his zeal for the Law — before declaring that all of this is "loss" compared to knowing Christ. The use of the term "eighth day" is not trivial: it is evidence of faithful family piety, right from the child's birth.
G3637.portee: This word reminds the reader that before becoming an apostle of Christ, Paul was an exemplary observant Jew. The precise mention of circumcision "on the eighth day" shows the importance of the details of the Law in the spiritual formation of a pious Hebrew. For today's Christian, this passage illustrates how Paul abandons his external and legal merits to fully trust in Christ — he questions everything, even what seemed to be the most fundamental mark of Jewish religious identity.

sens: the whole number that comes after seven
a period of eight days
G3638.detail:
1. The whole number that comes after seven. It is the simplest number: it designates a precise quantity of people or things. John 5:5 speaks of a man who had been ill for thirty-eight years, and Acts 9:33 mentions a paralyzed man who had been bedridden for eight years.

2. A period of eight days. In biblical language, "eight days" often designates a period that includes the day before and the day after a complete week, marking a new beginning. Jesus prayed on the mountain about eight days after speaking of his coming (Luke 9:28), and he appeared to his disciples eight days after his resurrection (John 20:26), inaugurating a new presence.
G3638.origine: The Greek word ὀκτώ comes from an ancient Indo-European root, the same as the Latin "octo" or the French "huit." It is a number that has no particular religious etymology: it is simply the natural number. In the Bible, however, eight has a subtle symbolic hue: it often represents a new beginning or a transcendence beyond the cycle of seven days.
G3638.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Acts. It designates precise durations: thirty-eight years of illness (John 5:5), eighteen years of spiritual captivity (Luke 13:16), eight years of infirmity (Acts 9:33). It also qualifies the specific day of circumcision (Luke 2:21) — the eighth day according to the Law — and marks the two appearances of the risen Lord: about eight days after the transfiguration (Luke 9:28) and exactly eight days after Easter (John 20:26). The context remains always concrete and historical.
G3638.portee: The number eight reminds the reader that Jesus respected the Law by presenting himself at the Temple on the eighth day, confirming that he did not come to abolish it. The Lord's appearance eight days after the resurrection emphasizes that divine power extends beyond the ordinary week, inaugurating a new time. These temporal precisions give the Gospel narrative reassuring historical solidity: the events are not vague myths, but dateable and verifiable facts.

sens: complete destruction, collapse
sudden and inevitable annihilation
eternal perdition, definitive punishment
moral and spiritual decay
G3639.detail:
1. Ruin designates the total collapse of a reality, whether physical or spiritual: the complete destruction of what was established. In 1 Corinthians 5:5, Paul speaks of the "destruction of the flesh," meaning the annihilation of carnal impulses through discipline.

2. The word evokes what happens suddenly and inevitably, without escape: a catastrophe that falls upon someone. In 1 Thessalonians 5:3, "sudden ruin will surprise them" describes the day of judgment that will come unexpectedly upon those who say, "Peace and safety."

3. Applied to eternity, ruin means definitive perdition, punishment that never ceases: it is the eternal separation from God. In 2 Thessalonians 1:9, those who do not know God suffer an "eternal ruin, away from the presence of the Lord."

4. By extension, the word describes the process of moral decay that leads someone to their loss: foolish desires "plunge men into ruin and destruction" (1 Timothy 6:9).
G3639.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to destroy, to annihilate." It evokes the image of a building or edifice collapsing, hence the general idea of irreparable destruction. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates Hebrew words that denote devastation and ravage. The root itself carries the idea of complete dissolution, of reduction to nothingness.
G3639.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, always in a context of judgment or punishment. In 1 Corinthians 5:5, Paul uses it for church discipline aimed at salvation. In 1 Thessalonians 5:3, it describes the day of judgment that will surprise the unbelievers. In 2 Thessalonians 1:9, it qualifies the eternal punishment of those who reject the Gospel. In 1 Timothy 6:9, it designates the moral and spiritual ruin that covetousness provokes. In all these cases, the word carries absolute gravity: it is total and definitive loss.
G3639.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader of the reality of divine judgment and its irreversible consequences. It highlights the mortal danger of unbelief and distance from God. At the same time, in 1 Corinthians 5:5, it shows that even severe church discipline aims for salvation, not condemnation. Understanding the eternal stakes of our choices should motivate the believer to vigilance and faithfulness.

sens: One who believes little, who lacks trust in God
One who doubts in the face of difficulty or danger
One who is paralyzed by worry rather than trusting
G3640.detail:
1. This word refers to a person who has faith, but a weak, timid faith that does not truly rely on God. In Matthew 14:31, Jesus calls Peter a "man of little faith" when he doubts while walking on water — he began to believe, but his trust wavered as soon as he saw the storm.

2. It is faith that falters in the face of danger or uncertainty. In Matthew 8:26, the disciples are afraid during the storm, and Jesus rebukes them: "Why are you afraid, you of little faith?" They know Jesus and should trust Him, but fear paralyzes them.

3. It is also worry that takes the place of trust. In Matthew 6:30 and Luke 12:28, Jesus invites not to worry about clothing and food: if God clothes the flowers of the field, why be anxious? Doubting His providence is to have little faith. In Matthew 16:8, the disciples reason about the lack of bread instead of remembering that Jesus just fed the crowds — this is still little faith.
G3640.origine: The word comes from two Greek roots: "oligos" (little) and "pistis" (faith, trust). The Greek term conveys the Semitic Hebrew idea of trust in God — not a theoretical belief, but a surrender to His goodness and power. To have "little faith" is to have this trust in insufficient, weakened quantity.
G3640.emploi: This word appears only five times in the New Testament, all in the Gospels, and always on the lips of Jesus. Jesus uses it to rebuke His disciples or listeners. Peter receives it while walking on water (Matthew 14:31), the disciples during the storm (Matthew 8:26) and because of their forgetfulness of the miracles (Matthew 16:8), the crowd in Matthew 6:30 and Luke 12:28 who worry about clothing and food. It is always in a moment where fear, doubt, or worry should have given way to trust in Jesus or in God's providence. The tone is gentle: Jesus does not condemn, He awakens.
G3640.portee: This word invites the Christian to examine his faith. Believing is not just accepting a doctrine; it is truly trusting God in trials, uncertainty, and need. Jesus expects His disciples to grow in trust. Each rebuke of "you of little faith" is also a promise: it is possible to grow, to move from doubt to confident surrender. For today's reader, it is an invitation to ask God to strengthen his faith, especially in times when worry and fear threaten.

sens: Small in number or quantity
Small in importance or value
Short in time
Short in space
Almost, barely (in specific constructions)
G3641.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning refers to what is few in number or scarce: a few people, a small quantity. Jesus says that "few" find the narrow gate (Matthew 7:14), and there was "little" bread to feed the crowd (Matthew 15:34).
2. The word also expresses what is small in importance or value, what matters little. The faithful servant who is "faithful in a little" receives greater responsibility (Matthew 25:23): what he managed was modest, but his merit is great.
3. Used for time, it means a short duration. Jesus asks His disciples to rest "a little" (Mark 6:31), or Paul is "soon" persuading Agrippa (Acts 26:28).
4. For space, it indicates a small distance. Simon moves "a little" from shore when Jesus gets into his boat (Luke 5:3).
5. In certain constructions, it takes on a nuance of approximation or near-certainty: "you are almost persuading me" means "you are nearly persuading me."
G3641.origine: The word comes from an ancient Greek root related to the idea of limitation. It regularly translates the Hebrew מָעַט (meʿat), which carries the same sense of smallness or scarcity. It is a simple and ancient adjective in common Greek vocabulary.
G3641.emploi: The word "little" appears about 41 times in the New Testament, in almost all books, especially the Gospels and the epistles. It is used concretely for quantities, numbers of people, and measures (bread, wine, distance), but also abstractly for material goods, time, or importance. Sometimes it retains its purely numerical value ("few" disciples), and sometimes it becomes almost adverbial to express brevity or approximation (Acts 26:28: "you are almost persuading me"). Acts 12:18 shows a particular translation: "great commotion" where the Greek says "not a little commotion," meaning "much."
G3641.portee: This word invites the believer to see that the perspectives of the kingdom of God overturn the standards of the world. "Few" find the narrow way, but those who find it possess the essential. Being faithful in "little" is already an act of value before God. The word also reminds us of the brevity of earthly life (James 4:14) and urges us to consider its spiritual importance.

sens: Who has lost courage, self-confidence, or hope for the future
Who is discouraged, lacking moral strength in the face of trials
G3642.detail:
1. The word depicts someone whose heart has weakened, who has lost confidence in the face of life's difficulties. It describes the state of one who sees no way out, who doubts. In 1 Thessalonians 5:14, Paul urges Christians to "encourage the downcast" — referring to believers discouraged by persecution or by the wait for Christ's return.
2. More broadly, it indicates a lack of inner strength, a moral weakness that renders someone unable to stand firm or move forward. It is the opposite of courage and trust in God.
G3642.origine: The Greek word combines two roots: "oligos" (little, small) and "psychè" (soul, heart). The image is of a soul shrunk, emptied of its strength, as if the heart had diminished. The same idea is found in Hebrew, where Isaiah 35:4 speaks of a heart that weakens before God.
G3642.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Thessalonians 5:14, where Paul gives practical instructions for community life. It specifically refers to those whose morale has fallen, who have lost confidence — and he calls strong Christians to lift them up through encouragement and support. The context shows that this downcast state is not a shameful weakness, but a real condition that the community must recognize and care for with tenderness.
G3642.portee: This word reminds the reader that downcast and discouragement are legitimate human realities, even in faith. It also teaches that it is a Christian duty to recognize those who are faltering and to support them through words, prayer, and patience — not through criticism, but through brotherly consolation.

sens: To hold in little regard, consider unimportant
To reject with disdain, treat with contempt
To neglect or ignore deliberately
G3643.detail:
1. The word denotes the action of considering something as unimportant, worthless. It means to regard lightly, to take lightly. In Hebrews 12:5, Paul exhorts his readers: do not despise the Lord's discipline — that is, do not treat it as negligible or unworthy of attention, even when it is painful.
2. Despising goes beyond indifference: it is a form of rejection or disdain. To despise is to refuse to give weight to something, to reject it as unworthy.
3. To despise can also mean to deliberately neglect, to turn a blind eye to something important. When one despises divine correction, one deliberately ignores it, refusing to listen.
G3643.origine: The Greek word ὀλιγωρέω is formed from ὀλίγος (little, few) and ὤρα (care, attention). The image is this: to give little care to something, to pay little attention. In Hebrew, the Old Testament (Proverbs 3:11 in the Greek version) uses the verb מָאַס (mas), which also means to reject or despise. This group of words (ὀλίγος, ὀλιγοψυχέω, etc.) shares the common idea of "little" or "weak," expressing a lack of esteem or effort.
G3643.emploi: The verb ὀλιγωρέω appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 12:5. Paul quotes the passage from Proverbs to warn Christians not to despise divine correction — which would be a serious spiritual fault. The context is that of God's discipline: because He loves us, God disciplines us. To despise this discipline is to refuse to recognize its educational value and the love that is its source. It shows a culpable lightness in the face of what God does for our good.
G3643.portee: This word reminds us that divine correction is never an arbitrary punishment, but a proof of love. To despise this correction is to lose sight of God's fatherly character toward us. For the believer, the challenge is not to take lightly what God teaches us through difficulty, suffering, or warning — it is to recognize in these moments the hand of a Father who wants our good.

sens: one who destroys or kills en masse
the angel or power that executes divine judgment
G3644.detail:
1. The destroyer is primarily one who destroys, who kills, who annihilates: the word evokes a destructive force that acts with power and without mercy. In 1 Corinthians 10:10, Paul refers to the angel who struck the Israelites in the desert: "who perished by the destroyer" — it is the agent of God's judgment.
2. In a figurative and biblical sense, it is the divine power itself that executes destruction: the destroyer does not act on its own will, but as an instrument of judgment. This word shows that God never destroys without reason, but by a force sent deliberately against those who defy Him.
G3644.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb ὀλοθρεύω (olothreúô), which means "to destroy completely, to annihilate." This verb itself comes from the Greek root that expresses the idea of complete ruin, total destruction. In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses words like שׁחת (shâkhath, "to destroy") or דברה (dâbhâh, "to speak, to utter") to express a destruction that comes from God; the Greek word olothreutês captures this divine force of annihilation.
G3644.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 10:10. Paul cites a passage from the Exodus narrative: the Israelites murmured against God in the desert, and God sent against them the "destroyer," that is, an angel who executed His judgment and killed them. Paul uses this rare and solemn term to remind the Corinthians of the seriousness of murmuring and rebellion against God: those who oppose His will expose themselves to His fearsome judgment.
G3644.portee: This word reminds believers that God's judgment is not a vague abstraction: it is a real and terrible force that strikes those who provoke Him. Murmuring, ingratitude, rebellion are not minor sins — they attract judgment. But this reminder also serves a protective purpose: understanding that God judges and destroys iniquity helps the Christian to fear God and walk in obedience rather than rebellion.

sens: one who destroys or annihilates
one who kills
the angel or divine power that executes judgment
G3645.detail:
1. The word designates one who completely destroys or annihilates. It is a being or force that brings ruin and death. In Hebrews 11:28, it refers to the destroyer who is about to strike the firstborn of Egypt: a power of destruction sent by God.

2. More specifically, it is one who kills, who takes life. The context of the tenth plague in Egypt shows that it is a fearsome and irresistible agent of death.

3. In a biblical perspective, the destroyer is often the angel or divine power that executes God's judgment. It does not act on its own initiative, but as an instrument of divine will to punish evil and deliver God's people.
G3645.origine: The word comes from the Greek root ὄλεθρος (olethros), which means "destruction," "ruin," "death." The verb ὀλοθρεύω is a later derivative, created to express the action of destroying. In translating the Greek Old Testament, this word renders the Hebrew כָּרַת (karat, "to cut off") and שָׁחַת (shachat, "to destroy"), which describe complete annihilation. The family of the word always evokes the idea of total and irreversible destruction.
G3645.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 11:28, where it designates the destroyer of the tenth plague in Egypt. In this passage, the author of the epistle recalls how Moses, by faith, instituted the Passover and the sprinkling of blood on the doorposts: thanks to this sign, the destroyer did not touch the firstborn of the Israelites. This context shows that the word evokes a superhuman, terrible, and irresistible power tasked with executing divine vengeance. The passage emphasizes faith as the only protection against this judgment.
G3645.portee: This word reminds Christians of the reality of divine judgment: God can send death and destruction upon those who reject Him. But Hebrews 11:28 also teaches that faith and obedience — symbolized by the blood of the lamb — offer sure protection. For the believer, it is an invitation to fear God and rely on His grace to escape judgment.

sens: sacrifice where the victim was entirely consumed by fire
offering that ascended entirely to God in smoke
act of total devotion to God
G3646.detail:
1. The burnt offering is a sacrifice where the animal offered (usually a lamb or a bull) was completely burned on the altar; nothing was kept for the food of the priest or the people. This totality expressed the entire gift of the victim to God (Hebrews 10:6).
2. The word paints the image of smoke rising entirely to heaven, which meant that the offering ascended fully to God. That is why the burnt offering was the quintessential symbol of unreserved devotion.
3. Figuratively, Jesus in His death became the perfect burnt offering: like the animal burned on the altar, He offered Himself completely for our sins. Mark 12:33 shows that Jesus taught that loving God with all one's heart is better than all material burnt offerings.
G3646.origine: The word comes from the Greek "holos" (whole, all) and "kaio" (to burn). The Hebrew "olah" (offering that ascends) was translated this way into Greek in the Old Testament. This name reflects the central gesture of the sacrifice: completely consumed, nothing remained, everything ascended to God.
G3646.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, always to speak of the Old Testament. In Hebrews 10:6 and 10:8, it is cited from a messianic psalm to show that God never wanted material sacrifices for their own sake, but the submission of the heart. Mark 12:33 places the burnt offering among the practices of the old Law, which Jesus surpasses by asking for love from the heart. These three uses look back to the Old Testament and its fulfillment in Christ.
G3646.portee: The burnt offering reminds us that God does not expect from us mere external acts of purity, but the complete gift of ourselves: our heart, our mind, our soul, our strength. In Christ, this sacrifice is fulfilled definitively: He offered Himself entirely for us, and we are called to respond with total and unreserved love.

sens: State of one who is healed, made whole and sound after an illness or injury
Restored physical integrity, absence of pain or defect in the body
G3647.detail:
1. Healing is the complete restoration of health, the state of being fully restored. In Acts 3:16, the apostle Peter explains that the lame man who regained the use of his legs received this "healing" — not only does he walk again, but his entire body functions normally again, restored to its integrity.
2. The word emphasizes the idea of integrity, absence of rupture or defect. It is not just that the ailment disappears, but that the person is "whole," complete, without cracks — like a body returned to its original function and balance.
G3647.origine: The word comes from the Greek "holos" (whole, complete) and "kleros" (part, portion): literally "to have one's full share." It is related to the adjective "holokleros" (whole, without defect), which expresses the idea of a whole that has lost nothing. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew "metom" (integrity, perfection), which also evokes this notion of unviolated totality.
G3647.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 3:16. Peter uses it to describe the miracle of healing the lame beggar at the Temple gate: it is by faith in the name of Jesus that this man received his "complete healing." The context shows that this is not a partial improvement, but a total and visible restoration — the beggar who could not move now walks again, before all the apostles and the crowd.
G3647.portee: This word reminds us that the healing Jesus brings is not a temporary or incomplete repair, but a true restoration of the person in their integrity. It invites the believer to desire and expect from God a health and a whole life, marked not by defect or rupture, but by fullness — an echo of the biblical image of a living and functional body, returned to its original purpose.

sens: Which includes all parts, with nothing missing
Which is complete in its state or development
In ethics: conforming to what is right, without moral defect
G3648.detail:
1. The word first evokes physical or material integrity: something whole, where no part has been removed or damaged. In 1 Thessalonians 5:23, Paul wishes that the faithful be kept "whole" — that is, that their spirit, soul, and body remain intact and healthy until the return of Christ.
2. The word also designates what is completed, which has reached its goal or perfection. In James 1:4, patience must accomplish its work "perfectly," meaning to bring to completion its transformative work in the believer, until he is "perfect and complete."
3. In this ethical context, "whole" also means "without defect," "blameless," morally and spiritually conforming. It is the integrity of heart and conduct that God expects.
G3648.origine: The Greek word combines two roots: "holos" (whole, all) and "klêros" (what has fallen to share, a portion). The original image is that of something that includes the totality of what has been distributed or assigned — nothing has been taken away. The same family is found in French in "holo-" (entirely) and the word "part" or "sharing."
G3648.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament, always in Pauline letters or those of close disciples. In 1 Thessalonians 5:23, it expresses the wish that God sanctifies believers in their entirety — spirit, soul, and body — by keeping them whole and blameless. In James 1:4, it qualifies the final state of the believer who has allowed patience to accomplish its work: he is then "perfect and complete," lacking in nothing. The word thus carries a strong spiritual and moral significance, related to the perfection of the Christian and his integrity before God.
G3648.portee: This word invites the believer to understand that God's sanctification aims at the whole person — not just their soul or spirit, but also their body and concrete habits. It also reminds us that spiritual maturity is not fragmentary: it is a complete accomplishment, where no area of life is left behind. The patience and faithfulness of the Christian must bear fruit to the end, without half-measures.

sens: To utter sharp and lamentable cries
To weep loudly in distress or pain
To express deep suffering through groans
G3649.detail:
1. The word first paints the concrete image of a person uttering sharp cries, like an involuntary cry of pain or terror. It is a very raw, very physical expression of suffering.
2. In the biblical context, it is to weep loudly, not silently, but with audible groans — the kind of weeping that someone in great distress produces. In James 5:1, the rich who have exploited workers are called to "groan" upon seeing the misfortunes they have deserved coming upon them.
3. More broadly, the verb expresses a deep lamentation, the outward manifestation of an inner suffering that cannot be contained. It is a cry that comes from deep within oneself.
G3649.origine: The word is an onomatopoeia — it imitates the very sound of groaning or crying out in pain. This imitation of sound is so clear that it remains similar in many languages. In Hebrew, the verb יָלַל ("yalal") meaning to howl or lament produces a sound effect very close: the Greek Bible often uses it to translate this Hebrew cry. This resonance with the natural language of suffering explains why this verb is so expressive.
G3649.emploi: This verb is found only once in the New Testament, in James 5:1. The apostle James calls the rich who have amassed wealth through injustice to "groan" as they contemplate the misfortunes coming upon them — it is a cry of horror and despair before the judgment of God. The context makes it clear that this groaning is not a mere complaint, but a deep expression of distress in light of the consequences of their sins.
G3649.portee: This word reminds the reader that there is a justice of God that does not remain inactive. The rich who oppress the poor to accumulate goods will one day have to answer for their actions, and that day will be a day of distress for them. For the believer, this calls for vigilance: not to let the love of money corrupt our justice. For those who suffer unjustly at the hands of the dishonest, it is an assurance that God does not turn a blind eye.

sens: Which forms a complete unit, without division or lack (the whole of a thing)
Which encompasses every part, every element (the totality)
Which extends everywhere, to every place (universality)
Used with an adjective or verb to reinforce the meaning (entirely, completely)
G3650.detail:
1. The word describes a thing considered in its entirety, leaving no part aside. This is the contrast between a part and the whole: John 13:10 speaks of the body being "all" washed, meaning in its entirety. John 9:34 states that the man was born "all" in sin, emphasizing that this condition affects him completely, from top to bottom.
2. Applied to humans or places, it means "each, all without exception." Matthew 1:22 speaks of "all" that happened in fulfillment of the prophecy, meaning the entirety of events. Mark 1:33 reports that "all" the city gathered at Jesus' door: every inhabitant, or at least the entire crowd.
3. Used for regions or periods, it designates space or time considered without limit: Mark 15:33 mentions darkness over "all" the earth, from the sixth to the ninth hour — the entire domain is targeted. Acts 13:6 speaks of crossing "all" the island: from one end to the other.
4. When accompanying a verb or adjective, it reinforces the idea of an action or quality that applies without reservation. Luke 13:21 describes the leaven that permeates "all" the dough: the action is complete and thorough, nothing escapes it.
G3650.origine: The Greek word holos comes from an Indo-European root meaning "whole, intact." It is a fundamental adjective, used in the Septuagint to translate the Hebrew kol (כֹּל), which carries the same meaning. Holos is found in many related French words: "holism," "holograph," "catholicity" (from the Greek katholikos, "universal"). It is a very common term in ancient Greek, belonging to the basic vocabulary.
G3650.emploi: Holos is one of the most frequently used words in the New Testament: about 100 occurrences. It appears in all four Gospels and in Acts with a high density, less often in the Pauline epistles. In the Gospels, it qualifies entire crowds (Mark 1:33), regions (Matthew 4:23: "all of Galilee"), periods (Mark 15:33), or reinforces the integrity of a person (John 9:34). In Acts, it often expresses the universal expansion of the Good News (Acts 11:26: the disciples were "called Christians" everywhere in Antioch). The word can precede the article and noun, follow the noun with the article, or be placed between the article and the noun according to syntactical needs. Very rarely does it function as an adverb (John 19:23, "di'holou," "everywhere").
G3650.portee: This word invites the reader to grasp the scope of God's action: when the Good News spreads "everywhere," or when Jesus heals while crossing "all" a region, the totality of reality is affected. It is also a reminder that God acts without half-measures: He wants our heart "entirely" (Mark 12:30). For the Christian, "all" that exists — every person, every place, every moment — is called to enter the Kingdom.

sens: Which is complete in all its parts, with none missing
Which is perfect, finished, lacking nothing
G3651.detail:
1. The word designates something complete, where no part is omitted or imperfect. In 1 Thessalonians 5:23, Paul speaks of sanctifying the believers "entirely" — meaning that the process of sanctification must touch all dimensions of their being (spirit, soul, and body), leaving none aside.
2. Beyond simply being complete, the word evokes the idea of perfection and integrity: it is a state of total accomplishment, where nothing is lacking. The requested sanctification is not partial or superficial, but aims at the whole person in its entirety and integrity.
G3651.origine: The word is formed from two parts: ὅλος (holos, "all, whole") and τέλος (telos, "end, accomplishment"). This combination suggests a totality that reaches its end, a complete accomplishment. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, a similar idea is found with words meaning "integrity" or "perfection" (like שָׁלֵם, shalom). The Greek word ὁλόκληρος (holoklēros) shares a very close meaning, but ὁλοτελής emphasizes more the completion and fulfillment of each part.
G3651.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Thessalonians 5:23. Paul uses it to urge the Thessalonians to seek complete and unreserved sanctification. It appears in a context of prayer and vow: Paul prays that God sanctifies the believers "entirely," meaning that the work of the Holy Spirit transforms and purifies every dimension of their existence (body, soul, spirit) before the return of Christ. It is a rare but precise word to express the scope and radical nature of Christian transformation.
G3651.portee: This word reminds the Christian that sanctification is not a partial or superficial matter: it concerns the whole person. This means that our walk with Christ must affect our body (our actions and habits), our soul (our emotions and thoughts), and our spirit (our relationship with God). It is a call to complete moral and spiritual integrity, an invitation not to leave areas of life untouched by the transformation of the Holy Spirit. No part of ourselves should remain unchanged or dedicated to sin.

sens: Christian from Rome mentioned by Paul in his final greetings
G3652.detail: Olympus is a man to whom Paul sends greetings to the Christians in Rome. His name appears only once in the Bible, in the midst of a list of brothers and sisters in Christ to whom Paul expresses his affections — a sign of his importance in the Roman community, even though we know nothing else about him.
G3652.origine: The name Olympus likely comes from a contracted form of the Greek Olympiodoros ("given by Olympus" or "related to the Olympic Games"). It is a common Greek name in the Roman Empire, borne by slaves and people of modest means, which fits with the context of the Christian community in Rome — a mix of people from all backgrounds and conditions.
G3652.emploi: Olympus is mentioned only once, in Romans 16:15, in the final doxology of Paul's letter to the Romans. He is listed among about twenty names of Christians to whom Paul sends his personal greetings: Philologus, Julia, Nereus, his sister, and others. These greetings reveal that Paul knows and honors the brothers and sisters in Rome — showing that a living and well-established church already existed in the capital, well before his visit.
G3652.portee: The fact that Paul names Olympus shows that in the early Church, everyone counts. Olympus may not have been a famous leader or remarkable speaker, but Paul knows him, loves him, and wants him to be greeted — a lesson in brotherly tenderness and the importance of every link in the Christian community.

sens: Immature fig that grows in winter
Unripe fruit that generally falls in spring when shaken
G3653.detail:
1. The green fig is an immature fig that develops during the winter on the fig tree and has not had time to ripen. It is a small, still hard, and less flavorful fruit, very different from the ripe and sweet figs harvested in summer.
2. These green figs naturally fall in spring or are easily detached from the fig tree by a violent shock: in Revelation 6:13, a fig tree shaken by a powerful wind "drops its green figs," an image of the sudden and massive fall of the stars from heaven during eschatological judgments.
G3653.origine: The Greek word ὄλυνθος literally refers to the early or immature fig. In Hebrew, the word פַּג (pag) from Song of Solomon 2:13 describes the same reality: a fig that grows out of season and does not reach maturity. The image comes from agricultural observation: the fig tree naturally produces a small early harvest in winter, meant to fall or be eaten before the true summer harvest.
G3653.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 6:13. John uses it in his eschatological vision to describe the stars falling from heaven "like a fig tree shaken by a violent wind drops its green figs." The chosen image — an immature and worthless fruit — emphasizes the sudden, massive, and definitive nature of the fall of celestial powers, with no possibility of recovery or usefulness for the coming judgment.
G3653.portee: This immature fig symbolizes the fragility and uselessness of realities that seem stable but are merely temporary. For the believer, the image serves as a reminder that the visible powers of the cosmos, however majestic, will suddenly collapse before the sovereignty of God. It is an invitation not to place trust in earthly systems or the apparent cosmic order, but solely in the Lord who remains after the fall of all things.

sens: completely, totally, without exception
truly, certainly, really
not at all (with a negation)
G3654.detail:
1. The word expresses totality, completeness: it means "entire," "in its entirety." When Paul says that the immorality being discussed exists "generally" (1 Corinthians 5:1), he means that it is known to all, recognized everywhere.
2. It can affirm a reality in a certain and solemn manner: "certainly, it is already a fault among you" (1 Corinthians 6:7) means that it is undeniably, authentically a problem.
3. Placed after a negation, it reinforces it and means "not at all," "in no way." Jesus says not to swear "at all" (Matthew 5:34): not a single oath, to no degree. Paul asserts that the dead do not rise "at all" (1 Corinthians 15:29), positing a condition for the absurdity of baptism for the dead.
G3654.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective ὅλος (holos), which means "whole, complete, all." It is an adverb formed from this root: it carries all the force of totality. The same root is found in French words like "holism" or "holo-" ("all"). This adverb thus expresses the idea that something is considered in its entirety, without reservation or exception.
G3654.emploi: This word appears four times in the New Testament, always in Paul or in the words of Jesus. With a negation, it reinforces the prohibition ("do not swear at all," Matthew 5:34, where Jesus refuses any oath). Without an explicit negation, it affirms a reality categorically or expresses a general notoriety ("it is generally said"). In 1 Corinthians, it appears three times to affirm realities concerning ethics or doctrine: the scandal of immorality, the failure to resort to courts, the absurd consequence if the dead do not rise. The word always carries doctrinal or moral weight.
G3654.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us of the radical nature of certain biblical teachings. When Jesus says "do not swear at all," it is a total requirement, not a mere recommendation. When Paul judges a situation "certainly" guilty, it is an unambiguous judgment. This word invites us not to dilute the Word, but to receive it in all its strength and clarity.

sens: Fall of water from the sky in the form of drops
Shower, passing downpour
In a figurative sense, that which falls from heaven like rain
G3655.detail:
1. The word refers to rain, this natural fall of water that comes from the sky in drops. It is the ordinary meteorological phenomenon that everyone knows. In Luke 12:54, Jesus invites the crowds to observe how a cloud in the west announces the rain that is coming: it is an observation of the sensible world that he uses for a deeper lesson.

2. Ombros can also describe a shower or downpour, that is, a sudden and often abundant rain, rather than a fine and lasting rain. The word emphasizes the intense or striking nature of the fall of water.

3. By figurative extension, the word can evoke anything that "falls" from heaven like rain — a blessing or a judgment sent by God upon the earth.
G3655.origine: The Greek word ombros comes from an ancient root that evokes the meteorological phenomenon itself. In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses several terms for rain (notably guéshem for ordinary rain and zérem for a downpour), and the Greek version of the Old Testament often translated these terms by ombros or similar words. Rain was a central concern in the ancient Near East, both for daily life and for biblical theology, as it symbolized divine blessing or judgment.
G3655.emploi: The word appears only once in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 12:54. Jesus addresses the crowds who know how to read the signs of the sky: when they see a cloud rising in the west, they immediately say that rain will come. This ordinary remark ("it happens this way") becomes the occasion for a more serious critique: the disciples can discern the meteorological signs, but they do not know how to discern the signs of the times or recognize Jesus himself as the ultimate sign of the coming Kingdom. The context shows that ombros is an expected, inevitable rain, inscribed in the order of nature — which makes it all the more ironic that the listeners do not recognize what is spiritually obvious.
G3655.portee: This passage invites each reader to ask a personal question: am I as attentive to spiritual signs as I can be to natural signs? Jesus urges us to use our ability to observe and discern — not only the clouds and the rain, but especially his own presence and God's calls in our lives. It is an exhortation to vigilance and spiritual intelligence.

sens: Being together and exchanging words
Talking with someone about a particular subject
Regularly conversing with someone
G3656.detail:
1. The word primarily describes the action of being in the company of others and conversing: it is being together and speaking together. To the disciples on the road to Emmaus, "they were conversing about all that had happened" (Luke 24:14) — they were walking together discussing recent events.
2. It also refers to speaking with someone on a specific topic. "While they were talking and discussing, Jesus approached" (Luke 24:15): two people exchange words, one turning to the other to engage in dialogue.
3. The word can finally express a regular conversation, a habitual interaction: Felix "sent for him quite frequently, to converse with him" (Acts 24:26), creating a relationship of repeated meetings with Paul.
G3656.origine: The Greek word comes from the root that denotes an assembly or a group of people together (ὅμιλος). To converse is therefore primarily to "be with a group" and naturally to "speak together." This image of communal life, of sharing presence with one another, is at the heart of the word.
G3656.emploi: The verb appears four times in the New Testament, always in a context of direct and personal dialogue. In the Gospel of Luke (24:14-15), Jesus joins two disciples who were conversing on the road to Emmaus — the verb emphasizes that they were actively exchanging thoughts about the day's events. In Acts, Paul "spoke for a long time" with the brothers in Troas (20:11), sharing his life and teaching; elsewhere (24:26), Felix regularly sought out Paul "to converse" with him. The verb always emphasizes common presence and the lively exchange of words, never a one-man show discourse.
G3656.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian faith is lived out in conversation, dialogue, and communion. The disciples grow by talking together about what God is doing; Paul strengthens the brothers through repeated conversations. To converse is to acknowledge that we need one another, that shared words enlighten and draw us closer. For us today, it is a call to cultivate those moments when we discuss our faith experiences together and help one another.

sens: the group of people one regularly associates with
the influence exerted by the people one lives with or associates with
G3657.detail:
1. A company is a group of people who meet, live together, or regularly associate — the association of one person with others. In 1 Corinthians 15:33, Paul speaks of "bad company" that "corrupts good morals," referring to those with whom one spends time and from whom one absorbs habits.
2. The word takes on a broader meaning: it is the concrete influence these people have on us. We are never unchanged when we live near someone; their words, actions, and ethics will affect us. Paul warns: regularly associating with unscrupulous people ultimately corrupts even those who had good habits.
G3657.origine: The Greek word comes from "omillos" (the crowd, the group). It is the word found in the Greek Old Testament to designate a company or assembly (for example in Exodus 21:10). The image is that of the group with which one mingles, with which one mixes.
G3657.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 15:33. Paul uses it in a warning addressed to the Corinthians, who live in the heart of a pagan city filled with temptations. His message is serious: one cannot remain innocent if one regularly surrounds oneself with people who have no scruples about doing wrong. "Bad company" is not just a bad influence — it actively destroys the good morals of those who associate with it.
G3657.portee: This verse speaks to every believer: tell me who you spend your time with, and I will tell you who you will become. It is an invitation to be cautious in choosing friends, environments, and those from whom we receive words and examples. Company is never neutral — it transforms us. For a young Christian especially, this means: cultivate friendships that will help you grow in faith, and distance yourself from what would lead you toward evil.

sens: a person who navigates the sea and makes a living from it
a member of a ship's crew
by extension, anyone who exploits or works the sea
G3658.detail:
1. A sailor is a person who lives from the sea and navigates it regularly — it is their profession and domain. In Revelation 18:17, alongside the pilots who steer the ships, the sailors are those who operate them, working the sails and rigging.
2. The word designates more broadly anyone who exploits the sea for a living: transporters of goods, fishermen, or dock workers. It is an entire class of people whose economy depends on maritime trade and navigation.
3. In the context of Revelation, sailors are depicted as witnesses to the fall of Babylon — they stand at a distance, horrified to see the collapse of the center of global trade they served.
G3658.origine: The Greek word ὅμιλος comes from a root indicating assembly or group. The primary meaning is the crowd, the multitude, before specializing to designate a professional group: sailors as a class of people living together from the same trade. In Hebrew, sacred texts also refer to those who work the sea, but the Greek word allows for a collective vision, like a crowd united by a profession.
G3658.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 18:17. John places it in an apocalyptic tableau: the destruction of Babylon, the great city of commerce. The sailors are depicted alongside the pilots and all those who became wealthy through the sea. Their horrified flight shows the collapse of the economic system that sustained them.
G3658.portee: This passage invites the Christian reader to meditate on the instability of earthly riches and human powers based on commerce. The sailors flee because their source of prosperity suddenly collapses; it is a call not to place trust in the empires or economic systems of the world, which pass away, but in the eternal kingdom of Christ.

sens: The organ of vision, the part of the body by which one sees
The act or capacity of seeing, the gaze
G3659.detail:
1. The word designates the physical organ of vision. In Matthew 20:34, Jesus touches the "eyes" of the two blind men to heal them: it refers to the anatomical organ, the very one that was afflicted by blindness.
2. By extension, it also designates the capacity to see and the living gaze. When speaking of the "eye" in a biblical sense, it evokes not only the physical structure but also the faculty of perceiving the world and the one who looks — a more spiritual and existential dimension.
G3659.origine: The Greek word ὄμμα comes from an ancient root designating the organ of vision. It is a poetic term in classical Greek. It translates the Hebrew עַיִן ("ayin") in the Greek texts of the Old Testament. This word belongs to the same family as "ὄψις" ("optics", appearance) and refers to the fundamental idea of "seeing" in Greek thought.
G3659.emploi: The word appears twice in the Gospels, both in accounts of miraculous healing. In Matthew 20:34, Jesus heals two blind men in Jericho by touching their eyes; in Mark 8:23, he heals a blind man from Bethsaida by putting saliva on his eyes and laying hands on him. In both contexts, ὄμμα strictly refers to the physical organ afflicted by blindness, the place where the miracle of restoring sight occurs. It is a medical and concrete vocabulary, typical of the evangelical narrative of miracles.
G3659.portee: These accounts of healing the eyes reveal Jesus' compassion for those who cannot see. Spiritually, the "eye" in the Bible often symbolizes the capacity to perceive divine truth and to follow Jesus. Healing the eyes restores not only physical vision but also the ability to "see" and follow the Lord — as confirmed by the attitude of the two blind men who "followed him" immediately after their healing.

sens: To affirm something under oath, invoking God or a sacred object as a guarantor of truth
To solemnly commit oneself by a vow or promise
To curse or utter imprecations
G3660.detail: 1. To swear is to affirm something solemnly by taking God or something sacred as a witness. One who swears exposes themselves to divine wrath if they lie. In Matthew 5:34, Jesus tells his disciples not to swear "either by heaven, for it is the throne of God": swearing by heaven is already invoking God Himself. 2. To swear can also mean to make a vow or solemn promise, a commitment that cannot be broken. In Hebrews 6:13, when God makes a promise to Abraham, "not being able to swear by a greater, He swore by Himself": this is an irrevocable promise sealed by an oath. 3. Sometimes, to swear takes on the meaning of cursing or violently accusing. In Mark 14:71, Peter "began to call down curses and to swear: I do not know this man": he reinforces his words with curses, not to affirm something before witnesses, but to violently reject the accusation.
G3660.origine: The Greek verb ὄμνυμι comes from a root meaning "to put forward" or "to solemnly promise." The Hebrew שָׁבַע (shabà), which Greek often translates, also refers to an oath. This verb belongs to the family of words related to commitment and given word, with similar forms in other ancient languages. The initial image is that of a word spoken with the highest solemnity, implying a sacred power.
G3660.emploi: The word appears about 20 times in the New Testament, mainly in Matthew and in the Epistle to the Hebrews. In Matthew, it is central to Jesus' teaching on oaths (5:34-37 and 23:16-22): Jesus forbids swearing by heaven, earth, Jerusalem, or one's head, for all of this belongs to God. In Mark and Luke, the verb describes concrete oaths: Herod swears to give half his kingdom (Mark 6:23), God swears to David (Luke 1:73). The Epistle to the Hebrews uses God's oath to show the absolute certainty of His word (3:11, 6:13-16, 7:21): when God swears, His promise is unbreakable. In James 5:12, swearing is discouraged, as in Matthew. The context shows an evolution: the Old Testament values the oath as a guarantee of truth, but Jesus forbids it to His disciples, who must be so honest that their simple word suffices.
G3660.portee: For the disciple, this word poses a radical question: is the quality of my word such that I do not need to swear to be believed? Jesus shifts the focus from the external form of the oath to inner integrity. However, Hebrews shows that God Himself swears to assure us of the immutability of His promises: our trust rests not on our fragile oaths, but on God's unbreakable oath. It is an invitation to radical sincerity and faith in God's word.

sens: With one and the same intention, one heart
Physically gathered in the same place, together
Acting or speaking in perfect harmony, with one voice
G3661.detail:
1. The word describes a deep unity of thought and will: several people have the same desire, the same goal. In Acts 1:14, the disciples and women "with one accord were devoting themselves to prayer" — they were not just praying at the same time, but with the same heart turned toward God. It is agreement in intention and commitment.

2. It also refers to the physical gathering of a group in the same place. In Acts 2:46, the believers were "together attending the temple" — they were physically present together, forming a visible community. This physical proximity reflects and strengthens their union.

3. The word finally emphasizes the common action or speech, the perfect coordination of a group. In Acts 4:24, when "all together" lift their voices to God, they pray with one voice; in Acts 7:57, the crowd rushes "all together" at Stephen — even if the act is reprehensible, the word shows that they act as one movement.
G3661.origine: The Greek word unites two roots: *homo-* ("same") and *thymos* ("heart, vital breath, intention"). The basic image is that of a single heart. It is a compound word forged to express not only "together" but "together of heart." It often translates the Hebrew *yacad* in the Greek Old Testament, which also means "together" and "in agreement." This Greek word hardly exists before the New Testament and biblical Greek literature: it arises from the desire to show a unity that is not only physical but spiritual.
G3661.emploi: The word appears 11 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in Acts (10 occurrences) and once in Romans 15:6. It characterizes the life of the early Church: common prayer (Acts 1:14, 4:24), daily fellowship (Acts 2:46), apostolic witness (Acts 5:12), even hostile reactions (Acts 7:57, 19:29). In Romans 15:6, Paul urges the Church to glorify God "with one voice." The word focuses on moments when the Church acts or prays collectively, showing that this unity is a constitutive trait of its life. It slightly shifts in nuance depending on the context: sometimes it is the deep agreement that matters (prayer), sometimes the physical presence (at the temple), but always the idea of a shared action or intention.
G3661.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reveals the ideal of the Church: not a collection of isolated individuals, but a body animated by one Spirit, one intention. It shows that unity is not a luxury or an ornament, but the reflection of the new life in Christ. In Acts, this harmony accompanies every advance of God's kingdom — prayer, growth, courageous witness. It invites today's believer to seek this unity of heart with their brothers, to pray "with one accord" rather than in isolation.

sens: To have the appearance of something or someone; to be similar to
G3662.detail: 1. The verb expresses visible similarity or appearance: something or someone has the traits, behavior, or aspect of another thing. In Mark 14:70, the servants of the high priest's house say to Peter: "You are also one of them; for you are Galilean, and your speech resembles it," meaning that his way of speaking makes him similar to the disciples, revealing him as a companion of Jesus.
G3662.origine: The verb comes from the Greek ὅμοιος (homoios), "similar," which carries the idea of resemblance or parity. It is a simple form of the verb "to resemble," more direct than the compounds (like "to appear to resemble"). The root expresses comparison and analogy, key concepts in Greek thought.
G3662.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Mark 14:70. It is used in a moment of dramatic tension: Peter, who has just denied knowing Jesus, is recognized by his way of speaking. The context shows that resemblance can be involuntary and revealing: it betrays someone's origin or belonging. This rare term emphasizes the strength of what makes us identifiable, even when we deny it.
G3662.portee: This word reminds us that our way of living, speaking, and acting manifests what resides within us. Just as Peter's way of speaking revealed him as a disciple of Jesus, our actions and words testify to our attachment to Him. We cannot hide if we truly belong to Him.

sens: Who has the same feelings, the same passions, the same conditions as another
Who shares the common human condition
G3663.detail:
1. The word describes someone who experiences the same feelings and needs as another person. In Acts 14:15, Paul and Barnabas remind the inhabitants of Lystra that they are not gods but men with the same human nature as them, with the same weaknesses and emotions — which makes their preaching credible and relatable.
2. It emphasizes that someone shares the ordinary human condition, without superhuman privilege. In James 5:17, Elijah is presented as a man of the same nature as us, to show that his powerful prayer was not the act of a superhuman being, but of an ordinary man in every way: this highlights his faith and obedience, not his exceptional nature.
G3663.origine: The word is composed of two Greek roots: ὅμοιος (homoios, "similar, alike") and πάσχω (paschô, "to suffer, to experience, to feel"). The basic idea is therefore one of sharing the same feelings and the same sufferings. This formation emphasizes the equality of human passions and conditions.
G3663.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Acts 14:15, Paul and Barnabas use it to distinguish themselves from idols and affirm their ordinary humanity. In James 5:17, it serves to remind that Elijah, despite his extraordinary power of prayer, was a man similar to us in his nature and human limitations. In both cases, the word refocuses attention not on superiority, but on an equality of nature that makes faith and obedience all the more remarkable.
G3663.portee: This word invites the reader not to place the apostles or great servants of God on an inhuman pedestal. Paul and Elijah are not superhuman beings, but ordinary men who believed and obeyed. This reality encourages us: if God acted through men like us, with the same weaknesses and emotions, our prayer and commitment can also bear fruit. It is an invitation to humility and trust.

sens: who has the same appearance, the same form
who has the same nature, the same qualities or abilities
who acts, thinks, or behaves in the same way
who can be compared to, who is akin to (in a comparison or parable)
G3664.detail:
1. Similar first refers to what strikes the eye: the outward appearance. In Revelation 1:13, the seer sees someone who "looked like a son of man," meaning whose general appearance resembled that of a man. The locusts in Revelation (9:7) "looked like horses," by their appearance and imaginary equipment.
2. Similar by deep nature, condition, abilities: what is at the heart of beings or things. In Galatians 5:21, Paul lists the "similar" sins - those that belong to the same family of evil. In 1 John 3:2, we will be similar to Jesus when we see him, meaning we will have the same essence, the same perfection.
3. Similar in the way of acting or thinking. In Matthew 11:16, Jesus says that this generation "is like" children who criticize the play of other children - same attitude, same whim. In John 8:55, one who claims not to know God would be "like" a liar, meaning would act like him.
4. Similar by comparison, in a parable or analogy. Matthew 13:31 ff lists several parables: "The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed... like leaven..." - Jesus brings two realities together to illuminate one by the other.
G3664.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and primarily denotes resemblance in form or appearance. It is formed from a root that evokes the idea of "same" (homo-). The Bible uses it to translate the ancient Hebrew כְּמוֹ ("like"): it is a key word for expressing comparisons and parables. Its family also includes the adverb "likewise" and the verb "to resemble."
G3664.emploi: This word appears 42 times in the New Testament, especially in Matthew, Luke, and Revelation. Matthew uses it abundantly in the parables of the kingdom (13:31-47, 20:1): Jesus compares the Kingdom to various earthly realities. Luke similarly takes it up (13:18-21). In Revelation, John uses it to describe heavenly visions (1:13, 4:6-7, 9:7-19): he seeks to express, through images, what escapes ordinary experience. The Apostle John (1 John 3:2) uses it theologically: being made similar to Jesus is the goal of faith. In Acts 17:29 and Galatians 5:21, it serves a moral logic: we are not similar to idols; some sins are similar to one another.
G3664.portee: For the believer, this word opens two paths. First, the parables of the Kingdom make it accessible: Jesus does not impose abstractions on us, he speaks to us through images similar to our life (the sower, the hidden treasure, the net cast into the sea). Second, the promise of 1 John 3:2 reminds us of our destiny: we will become similar to Jesus when we see him. This is the hope of the Christian - not an impersonal fusion, but a conformation to his holiness and love.

sens: Character of what is similar, of what resembles
Conformity or analogy between two things
Image or representation that imitates something
G3665.detail:
1. Resemblance is the common character shared by two things: it is what makes them similar or alike. In Hebrews 7:15, it is said that Melchizedek is a priest "in the likeness" of another, meaning he resembles him, sharing essential traits.
2. This word also denotes a conformity or analogy — a way of being similar without being identical. In Hebrews 4:15, Jesus was "tempted as we are in all things": there is a resemblance between his temptation and ours, a similarity in the nature of the trial, although he did not fall into sin.
3. More broadly, resemblance can be the image or representation that imitates a reality — what reproduces its visible or essential traits.
G3665.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective meaning "similar, alike." It primarily denotes the state or quality of what is similar: resemblance. In Hebrew, a similar idea is found with the word "kind" or "species" (used for creatures that reproduce according to their likeness in Genesis 1). The Greek suffix that ends this word is typical of abstract nouns designating a quality or state.
G3665.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, solely in the letter to the Hebrews. In Hebrews 7:15, it expresses how Melchizedek functions as an analogous priest, a figure resembling that of the Christ to come. In Hebrews 4:15, it emphasizes that Jesus experienced a temptation truly similar to ours — not a mere imitation, but a real resemblance — which makes him capable of sympathizing with our weaknesses. It is a word of theological thought, which helps express how one reality imitates or recalls another.
G3665.portee: This word reminds the Christian that Jesus is not a distant and inaccessible priest. Through his resemblance to us — his true experience of temptation — he understands our struggles and can help us. It is not a superficial resemblance, but a deep analogy that underpins his compassion for us.

sens: To become or be made like someone or something
To compare, to bring two realities together to show their resemblance
To take the form, appearance, or traits of
G3666.detail:
1. This verb expresses the idea of becoming like or being made like another. One can be similar to someone in a passive way (we are made similar) or in an active way (we become similar, we make ourselves similar). Jesus tells his disciples: "Do not be like them" (Matthew 6:8), meaning do not become like the hypocrites who pray to be seen. Elsewhere, the one who hears the words of Jesus but does not put them into practice "will be like a foolish man" (Matthew 7:26): he will take on the traits of dangerous folly.
2. This verb is also used to compare two things, to bring them together to show their resemblance: "To what shall we compare the kingdom of God?" (Mark 4:30). Jesus uses this method to teach: "The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed" (Matthew 13:24). Through this comparison, he makes a spiritual reality visible.
3. In the context of physical or moral resemblance, the verb can mean to adopt the form or appearance of another reality, as when the Son becomes like his brothers (Hebrews 2:17).
G3666.origine: The verb comes from the Greek adjective ὅμοιος (homoios), "similar, alike," which expresses resemblance and similarity. The root suggests an equality of appearance or nature. In Hebrew, the Old Testament primarily uses the verb דָּמָה (damah), "to resemble," to express the same idea. This Greek verb is used in parables, a literary genre that relies precisely on comparison: showing how a visible reality illuminates an invisible reality.
G3666.emploi: This verb appears 15 times in the New Testament, especially in Matthew (9 occurrences), who likes to use it to present the parables of the Kingdom. It is found in two main forms: first in the passive voice ("to be made similar, to become similar") when it concerns moral or spiritual conformity to a model; then in the active or middle voice ("to make similar, to compare") in the context of teaching through parable. In the parables of the Kingdom (Matthew 13:24, 18:23, 22:2, 25:1), Jesus uses this verb to introduce his comparisons: "The kingdom is like...". In Luke and Mark, it is used to formulate the question: "To what shall we compare the kingdom?" (Mark 4:30, Luke 13:18). In Matthew 6:8, "do not be like them," it is a moral warning. In Romans 9:29, Paul cites Scripture: "We would have become like Sodom," a negative likeness.
G3666.portee: This verb highlights how Jesus teaches through resemblance and comparison, making the Kingdom visible through images from the ordinary world. For the reader, it raises a lasting question: to whom or to what do you resemble? To become like someone is to adopt their traits, their values; the verb invites the believer to examine their moral and spiritual conformity. The parables of the Kingdom that use it reveal that divine reality is grasped through analogy with our experience.

sens: That which is similar, that resembles something
Image, concrete representation of something
Similarity, analogy between two realities
G3667.detail:
1. The word primarily designates that which is similar or resembles something else. It conveys the idea of resemblance, of correspondence between two things. For example, in Romans 5:14, Adam is described as "the figure of the one who was to come" — there is a resemblance, an analogy between his sin and a certain transgression.
2. In a more concrete sense, it designates an image, a material representation of something. Romans 1:23 speaks of "images resembling corruptible man, birds, and four-footed animals" — statues or visual representations created to resemble a model.
3. The word also expresses the similarity or abstract analogy between two realities. In Romans 8:3, Jesus is sent "in the likeness of sinful flesh" — not sinful flesh, but flesh that resembles that of sinful men. Similarly, in Philippians 2:7, Christ manifested himself "in the likeness of men": he truly took on human form while remaining divine. In Romans 6:5, "if we have become united with him in the likeness of his death," the word expresses a real union in the resemblance of fate.
G3667.origine: The word comes from the verb "homoioô" which means to make similar, to resemble. It is built on "homoios" (similar), which is itself related to "homos" (the same). Thus, it is a resemblance that brings two things closer without necessarily identifying them. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates Hebrew words like "demout" (likeness, image) and "tavnit" (form, model), which denote what imitates or represents something.
G3667.emploi: This word appears six times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul's major epistles (three times in Romans, once in Philippians) and in Revelation. In Romans 1:23, it refers to the images of idols made by men. In Romans 5:14 and 8:3, Paul uses it to express a theological analogy: the resemblance of Adam's sin to our transgressions, and the resemblance of Christ's flesh to our sinful flesh — a similarity that is not identity. In Philippians 2:7, the term illuminates the mystery of the incarnation: Jesus truly takes on human form. In Revelation 9:7, it describes the appearance of locusts that resemble war horses. The word thus plays a key role in speaking of what is analogous without being identical.
G3667.portee: This term helps the believer understand central realities of their faith. It shows that man, created in the image of God, is not God himself — there is resemblance, not identity. It also sheds light on the incarnation of Christ: Jesus truly took on our human condition, resembling men, to save us from within. And it reveals God's plan: through our union with Christ in his death and resurrection, we become like him, conformed to his image. Thus, resemblance is not a pale reflection, but a profound theological reality.

sens: In the same way, identically
Similarly, just as much
Equally, with the same equality
G3668.detail:
1. In the same way, identically: The word describes an action or situation that occurs exactly like another, or that follows the same pattern. In Matthew 22:26, after recounting what happened to the first brother who died, Jesus says, "it was the same for the second, and for the third": each suffered the same fate. This conveys the idea of repetition or an exact parallel.

2. Similarly, just as much: The word introduces a second action or element presented on the same level as the first, without distinction. In 1 Peter 5:5, after exhorting the elders, Peter says, "likewise, you who are younger, be subject to them," applying the same principle of obedience and humility to the young as to the elders. This is a call for consistency between groups or behaviors.

3. Equally, with the same equality: The word emphasizes that what applies to one applies with the same force to the other, without favoritism or difference. In 1 Corinthians 7:3, Paul writes that the husband owes his wife marital affection, "and the wife likewise to her husband": it is the same duty, the same rights for both. Equality is clearly affirmed.
G3668.origine: The word comes from the adjective homoios (similar, alike), formed from the root that expresses resemblance and identity.
