It carries the idea of doing in the same way, treating equally. The adjective appears notably in Matthew 13:33, where Jesus says, "The kingdom of heaven is like leaven." The adverb homoiôs is its adverbial form, transforming the idea of resemblance into that of an action or situation that repeats identically.
G3668.emploi: This adverb appears 31 times in the New Testament, mostly in Luke (10 occurrences), Matthew, and in the epistles. It serves to mark continuity, repetition, or equality between two or more elements. In Luke, it connects events in the narrative (Luke 6:31, 10:37: the good Samaritan acts likewise). In Matthew, it creates didactic parallels or enumerations (Matthew 22:26: the seven brothers). In the epistles, it applies a principle to several recipients or situations (1 Peter 5:5: the young as the elders; 1 Corinthians 7:3-4: the husband and wife). The word also appears in contexts of imitation (John 5:19: the Son does likewise as the Father) or of repeating the same suffering (Romans 1:27: men likewise abandon natural relations). It sometimes marks an escalation or reinforcement (Mark 15:31: the chief priests, likewise with the scribes, mock).
G3668.portee: This word reminds Christians of the importance of equality and justice in the application of God's Word: what applies to one applies to the other (Galatians 3:28). It also invites imitation: to do as Jesus did, to act towards others in the same way one would want to be treated. It is a call to ethical consistency and fraternal solidarity.

sens: The resemblance or outward appearance of a person
The state of one who has been made similar to someone else
The physical or conceptual representation of a reality
G3669.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes visible resemblance, what makes one person look like another — the appearance or features that can be seen. In James 3:9, Paul speaks of men made in the "image" of God: they bear the mark of the Creator who fashioned them in His likeness.
2. The word can also express the process or result of making someone similar to a model — the action of transforming someone to become like another. This conveys the idea of acquired or imposed conformity.
3. More broadly, it is the representation of a reality: what expresses, figures, or makes visible something abstract or invisible, like the divine essence reflected in the creature.
G3669.origine: The word comes from the verb homoioô ("to make similar, to resemble") which is based on the root homoios ("similar, alike"). In the Greek of the Old Testament, homoiôsis often translates the Hebrew word demout, which literally means "form" or "likeness" — showing that the biblical idea of man created "in the image of God" was already present in the Greek language of the Septuagint.
G3669.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in James 3:9. In this verse, the apostle recalls a troubling paradox: the same mouth that blesses God (which proclaims His greatness) curses men created in His image. This unique occurrence underscores the theological importance of the subject: man bears the divine image, and thus cursing him is an offense against God Himself. The context speaks of the tongue and its destructive power, which makes it all the more serious to curse those who reflect the character of the Creator.
G3669.portee: This notion reminds the Christian reader that every person, even those one might be tempted to despise or curse, bears the divine imprint. To respect and honor others is to honor God whose image shines in each. It is a powerful biblical foundation for rejecting slander, insult, and any words that demean human dignity.

sens: To openly say, to publicly declare
To acknowledge a fact, an act, a responsibility
To affirm a belief, a position
To confess one's sins before God
To praise, to celebrate
G3670.detail:
1. To openly say something in public, without fear or hesitation. In Matthew 7:23, Jesus says He will declare openly to sinners: "I never knew you" — a direct and clear word spoken face to face.
2. To acknowledge a fact or reality, to admit it. In Hebrews 11:13, the ancients "acknowledged" that they were strangers on the earth — they embraced this truth.
3. To affirm a doctrinal belief or a heartfelt position. In Acts 23:8, the Pharisees "affirm" the resurrection, while the Sadducees deny it — this is an opposing profession of faith.
4. To recognize and confess one's sins to God in order to obtain His forgiveness. In 1 John 1:9, "if we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us." 
5. To praise and celebrate God. In Hebrews 13:15, "let us offer through Him a sacrifice of praise, a confession of His name" — this is an act of recognition and glorification.
G3670.origine: The word comes from two Greek roots: "homo" (same) and "logos" (word). It literally means "to say the same thing," "to speak with one voice." The initial image is that of agreement: two people or one person and another speaking together, recognizing the same reality. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the verb "yadah" (raised hand, acknowledgment) or "neder" (vow, promise).
G3670.emploi: This word appears 23 times in the New Testament, mostly in the epistles of John and in the gospels. Jesus uses it to say that He will recognize those who recognize Him (Matthew 10:32; Luke 12:8). John the Baptist "declares" that he is not the Christ (John 1:20). Paul teaches that confession with the mouth leads to salvation (Romans 10:10): it is a word that engages the whole being. The epistles emphasize the confession of the Son (1 John 2:23), of the incarnate coming of Jesus (1 John 4:2), and the confession of sins (1 John 1:9). The word thus denotes a free, courageous, and engaging word — one that acknowledges the truth of God.
G3670.portee: To confess is to come out of hiding and take a stand: to recognize Jesus before others, to admit one's sins, to affirm one's faith openly. It is a word that binds the one who utters it — it expresses what he believes with all his heart and what he is ready to live. For the Christian, it is primarily an act of spiritual courage: to confess Jesus as Lord in a world that rejects Him. It is also an act of humility: admitting one's sins opens the door to God's forgiveness.

sens: Public declaration of what one believes or affirms
Explicit acknowledgment or recognition before witnesses
Commitment to firmly uphold a set of convictions
G3671.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the act of publicly and openly stating what one believes: in 1 Timothy 6:12, Timothy made "a good confession in the presence of many witnesses," meaning he declared his faith in Christ before others. It is a spoken word, heard, which commits the one who says it.
2. The profession of faith can be what one affirms or guarantees: in 2 Corinthians 9:13, the Corinthians are praised for "their profession of the Gospel of Christ," in other words, for the way they publicly confess and proclaim the Gospel. It is also what is manifested outwardly.
3. The word also describes the attitude of firmly and relentlessly holding a conviction: in Hebrews 10:23, we are told to "hold fast the profession of our hope," like grasping something precious and refusing to let go. It is a maintained, persevering affirmation.
G3671.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to say the same thing" or "to agree": homo- (same) and logia (word). The meaning evolves: first an agreement or contract where two parties "say the same thing" together, then it designates one who "says the same thing" as God, that is, who acknowledges and proclaims the truth of God. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, this word often translates as "vow" or "freewill offering," showing that a profession of faith among the Hebrews was already a personal and voluntary act by which one committed oneself.
G3671.emploi: The word appears six times in the New Testament, all in the epistles (2 Corinthians, 1 Timothy, Hebrews). It always describes the act of proclaiming or maintaining one's faith in Christ: in 1 Timothy, Jesus himself made "a good confession before Pontius Pilate," confirming who he was to the end. In Hebrews 3:1 and 4:14, it refers to "the faith we profess," as something that Christians state and hold together. The context always emphasizes the public or solemn aspect: it is speaking before witnesses, it is an act that costs and matters.
G3671.portee: For the Christian, this word invites one to clarify and boldly affirm publicly what they truly believe: it is not just an inner thought, but something that must be said and maintained. Just as Jesus confessed who he was before Pilate, and as Timothy did before witnesses, the believer is called to "confess" Jesus Christ without shame, even when it is difficult. It is ultimately an exhortation to perseverance: a profession of faith is only valuable if one "holds it firmly."

sens: In a confessed manner, recognized by all without dispute
In accordance with an agreement, with unanimous consent
G3672.detail:
1. This word designates what is openly recognized, admitted by all without possible contradiction. In 1 Timothy 3:16, Paul asserts that the mystery of godliness — that is, the secret of the Christian religious life revealed in Christ — is "without controversy" great: no one can seriously contest this fundamental truth. The adverb emphasizes the obviousness and unanimity of judgment.
2. The word can also express agreement, conformity with what has been jointly consented. It conveys the idea of something done "by common consent," in harmony with shared recognition.
G3672.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "homologeô" which means "to confess, to acknowledge, to say the same thing." The root "homo" (same) + "loge" (word) evokes the image of one who speaks with one voice as others. The adverb adds the sense of "in a confessed manner." It is a classical Greek formation to express what is unanimously recognized.
G3672.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 3:16. Paul uses it to introduce a key doctrinal text — presumably an ancient hymn or formula of faith — about the mysteries of the incarnation and exaltation of Christ. The adverb "without controversy" guarantees that the truths enumerated (manifestation in the flesh, justification by the Spirit, vision of angels, preaching to the nations, faith of the world, elevation in glory) are not disputable opinions, but realities confessed by the entire Church.
G3672.portee: This word reminds the reader that the Christian faith is not an isolated or doubtful opinion: it rests on truths recognized and confessed by the entire people of God. In reading it, the believer is invited to see in the mystery of Christ a reality so certain and manifest that it imposes itself on all who have opened their eyes — a trust that strengthens personal conviction.

sens: Who practices the same trade, the same profession as another person
G3673.detail: 1. The word designates two people who share the same trade or work. In Acts 18:3, Paul meets Aquila and Priscilla, a Jewish couple, and Scripture notes that he had "the same trade" as them: they were all tentmakers. This expression emphasizes a professional identity, a common point in the practice of the same craft or skill.
G3673.origine: The Greek word comes from two roots: "homos" (same) and "technè" (art, trade, skill). It literally designates one who practices the same art. The word "technè" evokes the idea of a skill acquired, a trade practiced with mastery, as opposed to improvisation or chance.
G3673.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 18:3. It is in this passage that Luke reports how Paul, arriving in Corinth after the vision of the night in Troas, meets Aquila and Priscilla. The fact that they shared the same trade created a natural bond between them: Paul settled with them to work. This usage shows how a professional affinity facilitated hospitality and fellowship among believers.
G3673.portee: This term reminds us that God honors human work, even manual labor, and that a common profession can create deep bonds among Christians. Paul, an apostle and theologian, did not deem it beneath him to work with his hands making tents: work dignifies the one who performs it faithfully. For us, it is a call to respect every honest profession and to see in our colleagues or fellow workers opportunities to witness and serve.

sens: In the same place, at the same time
In the same action or intention
With the same participation or sharing
G3674.detail:
1. The most direct meaning: several people or things in the same place or at the same moment. In John 21:2, seven disciples are "together" by the Sea of Tiberias; in Acts 2:1, the one hundred twenty believers are all "together" in the house where they are waiting for Pentecost. This conveys the idea of physical proximity.
2. "Together" also means to act in concert, sharing the same action. In John 20:4, Peter and John run "together" to the tomb — they make the same gesture, at the same moment, toward the same goal. This conveys the idea of common participation.
3. Without the idea of location, the word describes shared participation in a common joy or reality. In John 4:36, the sower and the reaper rejoice "together" — not necessarily in the same place, but in the same joy over the fruit they gather together. This conveys the idea of communion in a shared feeling or benefit.
G3674.origine: The word comes from the Greek root *homos* ("the same," "similar"). It is an adverb formed from this root, expressing the idea of gathering around an identity or equality. This root is found in other words like "homogeneous" or "homoousios" (in theology, "of the same substance"). The word always describes a gathering or participation born from this resemblance or uniqueness.
G3674.emploi: The adverb appears four times in the New Testament, all occurrences found in the Gospel of John and Acts. In John 21:2 and Acts 2:1, it describes a common physical presence: the disciples gathered in the same place. In John 20:4, it expresses a simultaneous action: two disciples running side by side. In John 4:36, it moves away from the idea of physical proximity to signify common participation in joy, a communion of feeling. The word is always linked to a unity, whether spatial, temporal, or moral.
G3674.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian life is never solitary. The disciples wait for Pentecost "together" because the power of the Holy Spirit unfolds in communion. The sower and the reaper rejoice "together" because the work of the Lord unites those who labor in it. "Together" invites the reader to seek unity in prayer, action, and joy — marks of the true Church.

sens: Who shares the same convictions and feelings
Who is united in spirit and judgment
Who manifests unity of heart and thought within a community
G3675.detail:
1. This word designates someone who thinks like others, who is not isolated in their convictions: a person "of one mind" with others walks in the same spiritual and moral direction. The image is that of a spirit (the Greek word φρήν literally refers to thought, the seat of judgment) that beats in rhythm with other spirits (1 Peter 3:8).

2. It is the inner unity that creates visible harmony: being of one mind means having crossed the threshold beyond mere tolerance to reach a true communion of heart and judgment among brothers and sisters of the same faith community.
G3675.origine: The word combines two Greek roots: ὁμός ("same, similar") and φρήν ("thought, spirit, heart"). It is a rare compound that concentrates the idea of mental and spiritual harmony. The root φρήν is found in other words that speak of inner attitude or judgment. This Greek term often conveys the Hebrew idea of unity and consent in one heart.
G3675.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 3:8, at the heart of an exhortation to community harmony. Peter addresses his readers, all "of one mind," alongside other qualities: brotherly love, compassion, and humility. The context shows that this unity of thought is not a flat or forced conformity, but the fruit of a heart converted to the same evangelical values. It is one of the essential conditions for living together in the Church.
G3675.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that Christian unity is not merely administrative or institutional: it begins in the heart and spirit. Being of one mind means accepting to let the Holy Spirit shape us together according to the same biblical convictions, the same spiritual priorities, and the same feelings of compassion toward one another. It is a call to end spiritual individualism.

sens: Expresses an opposition or restriction to what has just been said
Marks a concession: something is true despite an objection
Introduces a nuance or exception
G3676.detail:
1. This word introduces an objection or restriction to a previous statement. In John 12:42, "however" connects two opposing ideas: many leaders believed in Jesus, but "however" (despite this faith) they did not dare to confess it publicly for fear of the Pharisees. The adverb marks the contrast between what happens internally (faith) and what is manifested externally (silence).
2. The word can also express a concession or restriction in reasoning. In Galatians 3:15, Paul speaks of a human disposition or testament: although it is valid once established, it does not annul God's prior promise. The word nuances the reasoning by admitting a partial truth before establishing a greater one.
3. In some contexts, the word situates or places an idea "in the manner of" or "after the manner of": this is the case in 1 Corinthians 14:7, where the adverb has a value closer to "similarly" or "in the same way" — inanimate instruments, just like living beings, must produce distinct sounds to be understood.
G3676.origine: The word comes from a Greek root expressing resemblance or equality (ὁμός, "similar"). It is an adverb formed to denote a similarity or continuity of thought — hence its use to express a concession or logical restriction: one recognizes something as equivalent or similar while opposing a reservation.
G3676.emploi: This word is infrequent in the New Testament (only three occurrences in the Segond 1910). It appears in the Fourth Gospel (John 12:42) to express the psychological contrast of secret believers; in the letter to the Galatians (3:15) to nuance a theological argument about the antiquity of the divine promise; and in 1 Corinthians (14:7) where it plays a more particular syntactical role, as noted in the source definition. Its usage remains classically Greek: marking a gentle opposition, a concession, or a logical connection between two propositions.
G3676.portee: This word helps the reader perceive the real tensions of the Christian life: inner faith can coexist with external caution or restraint, without being a hypocritical contradiction — just human reality. It also teaches how to understand biblical reasoning: often they admit a partial truth ("however") before unfolding a broader perspective, thus marking the honesty and nuance of apostolic thought.

sens: Dream sent by God or nighttime vision during sleep
Divine message or warning received while sleeping
Appearance of an angel or person in a dream vision
G3677.detail:
1. A dream is primarily a natural experience of sleep, but in the Bible, it becomes the means by which God communicates with humans without using conscious words. Joseph receives the command to flee to Egypt: "an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream" (Matthew 2:13).
2. It is a warning or teaching that God conveys during the night, when the person is asleep and detached from earthly concerns. The wise men are "divinely warned in a dream not to return to Herod" (Matthew 2:12).
3. The vision of the dream may include an angelic appearance or a supernatural event perceived in this state. The angel who speaks to Joseph in a dream (Matthew 1:20) or Pilate's wife who "suffered greatly in a dream because of" Jesus (Matthew 27:19) testify to this visionary nature.
G3677.origine: The Greek word ὄναρ (onar) is an indeclinable noun — its form remains unchanged — and belongs to a small family of Greek words related to sleep and nighttime visions. It refers to the primary idea of what one sees when the eyes of the body are closed but those of the spirit remain active. In the Greek Old Testament, this word translates the Hebrew חלום (halôm), which refers to both ordinary dreams and divine revelations that come at night.
G3677.emploi: The word "dream" appears only six times in the New Testament, all in the Gospel of Matthew, and only to describe events related to the birth and childhood of Jesus. Matthew uses it to recount how Joseph receives the command to take Mary as his wife (1:20), how the wise men are warned not to return to Herod (2:12), how Joseph flees to Egypt (2:13), how he learns of Herod's death (2:19), how he withdraws to Galilee (2:22), and finally how Pilate's wife is troubled by a dream (27:19). In all cases, the dream is the channel through which God would guide or warn the characters without any words being spoken while awake.
G3677.portee: The dream reminds us that God does not need ordinary words to communicate with His children: He also acts in the invisibility and intimacy of sleep. For the Christian reader, this teaches spiritual vigilance: even when we sleep, God can speak to us. It is also an invitation to discern where God is at work beyond what is visible and rational.

sens: young donkey or little donkey
donkey used for light work or transport
G3678.detail:
1. A colt is a young donkey, or more broadly a little donkey — the Greek word is formed by a diminutive suffix that indicates smallness or youth. In John 12:14, during his entry into Jerusalem, Jesus rides on a colt, thus fulfilling an ancient prophecy.
2. This light animal was used for transport and travel: it is a humble mount, lacking the nobility of a horse, but reliable and docile for carrying a man on the roads or in the city.
G3678.origine: The Greek word ὀνάριον (onarion) is a diminutive of ὄνος (onos), which simply means "donkey." The suffix -άριον (-arion) is very productive in Greek for forming names of small beings or young beings: it creates a notion of reduced size or youth. The donkey is a well-known animal throughout the ancient world of the Middle East and the Mediterranean basin.
G3678.emploi: The word appears only once in the Greek New Testament, in John 12:14, during the solemn account of Jesus' entry into Jerusalem. This unique usage is highly significant: Jesus deliberately chooses a colt rather than a war horse, thus signaling the humility and gentleness of his reign. The youth of the animal could also emphasize its innocence and freshness. This detail fulfills the prophecy of Zechariah 9:9, where the king-messiah arrives on a colt.
G3678.portee: The colt on which Jesus enters Jerusalem embodies the contrast between the royal power expected of the Messiah and the humility with which he presents himself. This simple animal becomes a symbol of how Jesus establishes his reign: not by military force and glory, but by gentleness and submission to God's will. This invites the reader to rethink what it truly means to be a disciple of such a king.

sens: To address someone with offensive, humiliating, or mean words
To reproach someone for their conduct or unbelief
To treat someone with contempt in words or gestures
G3679.detail:
1. To insult means to hurt someone with harsh and offensive words. This is the most direct meaning: the robbers crucified with Jesus insulted him with words (Mark 15:32), as did the crowd (Matthew 27:44). Jesus' disciples should expect to be outraged — that is, insulted — because of their faith (Matthew 5:11, Luke 6:22).
2. To reproach means to address someone with a specific blame regarding their action or attitude. Jesus reproached the disciples for their unbelief and hardness of heart (Mark 16:14) because they did not believe he had risen. This is a reproach aimed at correction.
3. To reproach the cities means to criticize them, to publicly accuse them of their shortcomings. Jesus reproached the cities where he had performed miracles because they had not repented (Matthew 11:20). The insult can have a moral aim: it denounces an evil.
G3679.origine: The word comes from the ancient Greek « onéidos » (ὄνειδος), which means "reproach" or "insult." It is the reproach that brings shame. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, this word primarily translates the Hebrew « hareph » (חָרַף), which means "to defy," "to challenge," or "to address reproaches" with a tone of contempt or challenge.
G3679.emploi: The verb appears nine times in the New Testament. Matthew and Mark use it to describe the insults directed at Jesus during his Passion: those who are crucified with him insult him, as does the crowd. Luke and Matthew also use it for the insults that the disciples will suffer because of Christ. Mark and Matthew make it a verb of reproach: Jesus reproaches the disciples for their unbelief, and he reproaches the cities for their impenitence. In Romans 15:3, Paul cites a psalm where Jesus suffers the reproaches of the people. The word can refer to the brutal insults of the executioners or the more serious reproaches of a master who warns.
G3679.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that following Jesus can attract insults and contempt from the world (Matthew 5:11). But it also invites humility: correcting someone for their faults should be done not out of malice, but to correct, as Jesus did with his disciples. The word also shows us that Jesus himself suffered reproach and insult in our place — it is an act of obedience to God the Father.

sens: Insult, mockery, or derision directed at someone
Shame, dishonor, or bad reputation resulting from it
Public contempt, humiliation inflicted publicly
G3680.detail:
1. Opprobrium is primarily the insult or outrage inflicted on someone: mockeries, hurtful words, malicious reproaches (Romans 15:3: "The reproaches of those who reproach you"). It is the harm said about someone, the verbal attack or expressed contempt.
2. Opprobrium is also the shame and dishonor that follow: the bad reputation, the loss of credit and honor (1 Timothy 3:7: not falling into opprobrium to avoid a bad image). It is the result of the insult, what pursues you.
3. Finally, it is the public humiliation suffered: being despised in public, exposed to the judgment of others (Hebrews 10:33: "exposed as in a spectacle to reproaches"). The word images here a person dragged into ridicule before all.
G3680.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb ὀνειδίζω (to insult, to reproach), formed from a root that expresses the idea of reproach or blame. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it chiefly translates the word חֶרְפָּה (herpah, which also means insult or shame), which God knows well as a victim of human contempt. The family also includes the adjective ὀνειδέος (shameful) and the verb from which it derives.
G3680.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament, concentrated in Paul's epistles and the epistle to the Hebrews. Paul uses it to speak of Christ's suffering (Romans 15:3), who bore the insults in our place. The epistle to the Hebrews takes it up to describe the sufferings of early Christians (10:33) and, remarkably, to celebrate Moses' decision (11:26): he considered the reproach of Christ as a greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt — a prophetic passage where Moses already unites, by faith, with the shame of the future Christ. In 13:13, opprobrium becomes the honor of the disciples: "by bearing his reproach," that is, by accepting to suffer humiliation with Jesus. The word always denotes suffering, but gradually, it reveals itself as a path to glory.
G3680.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that Jesus bore our opprobrium; he accepted the insult and shame for us. But it also calls us not to be ashamed of this opprobrium: to follow him is to accept to share in his public humiliation, and this humiliation, viewed by faith, becomes a greater wealth than gold (as for Moses). It is a call to reverse the values of the world: where the world sees shame, faith sees the glory of the Cross.

sens: Reproach, blame directed at someone
Dishonor, public shame attached to a person or situation
G3681.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the reproach or blame directed at someone — the criticism, the disapproval they endure. It is the word that condemns and belittles.
2. More broadly, it is the dishonor and public shame that result, the bad reputation one carries in the eyes of all. In Luke 1:25, Elizabeth speaks of the opprobrium of being barren: it is the scorn and contempt that others directed at her because she could not have children.
G3681.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes the idea of wounding or striking morally. In Hebrew, it primarily translates חֶרְפָּה (herpa), which means reproach and shame. It is a strong word that expresses not only the judgment against someone but also the moral suffering they experience from it.
G3681.emploi: The word appears only once in the Gospel according to Luke (1:25). Elizabeth uses it when speaking of her barrenness: she was considered dishonorable because she had no children, which was a form of curse in Jewish thought. When she becomes pregnant with John the Baptist, she says that the Lord has removed her opprobrium — he has taken away this public shame and reproach.
G3681.portee: This word reminds us that God sees those who suffer from the contempt or judgment of men. Elizabeth bore the opprobrium of barrenness, but God looked upon her distress and exalted her. It is a promise for all who endure shame or rejection: God can reverse their situation and lift them up.

sens: Freed Christian slave, disciple of Paul
Bearer of an apostolic letter addressed to Philemon
G3682.detail: Onesimus is a slave who met the apostle Paul, probably in Rome, and converted to Christ. His name means "useful" or "profitable" in Greek — a common name among slaves in Roman times. Paul sends him with the letter to Philemon (Philemon 1:10), probably his master, to ask for his forgiveness and reinstatement, this time as a brother in Christ. Later, Paul mentions him again as "the faithful and beloved brother" sent to Colossae (Colossians 4:9), showing how this former slave became a respected collaborator in the early Church.
G3682.origine: The name Onesimus comes from the Greek ὄνησις (onèsis), which means "profit" or "advantage." It was a popular name given to slaves, sometimes ironically, since profitability was at the heart of their function in Roman households. The Pauline wordplay is subtle: by asking Philemon to receive Onesimus "no longer as a slave, but as a beloved brother," Paul transforms the meaning of the name — Onesimus truly becomes "useful" not through forced servitude, but through fraternal love in Christ.
G3682.emploi: Onesimus appears four times in the New Testament, all in Paul's epistles written during his captivity: twice in the short letter to Philemon (1:10 and 1:25) and twice in the one to the Colossians (4:9 and 4:18). The letter to Philemon is entirely devoted to his case: Paul intercedes for this runaway servant who has become a Christian, asking that Philemon receive him "no longer as a slave, but as a beloved brother." In Colossians, he is presented as a reliable messenger alongside Tychicus, showing the evolution of his status in the Church.
G3682.portee: The story of Onesimus illustrates the transforming love of the Gospel: a runaway slave, probably a criminal in the eyes of Roman law, is seized by the grace of Christ and becomes a cherished brother. For the reader, it shows that faith does not simply abolish social structures, but replaces them from within with relationships of mutual love. It invites us to see beyond human status to recognize the new dignity that Christ gives to every believer.

sens: Christian from Ephesus, faithful friend of the apostle Paul
G3683.detail: 1. Onesiphorus is a faithful follower of Christ encountered by Paul, probably in Ephesus. His Greek name literally means "one who brings advantage" or "one who profits" — a prophetic name that expresses his character: he has been a source of comfort and support for Paul.
G3683.origine: The name Onesiphorus comes from the Greek "onèsis" (advantage, profit) and "phorein" (to bear, to bring). It is a meaningful name, as was common among the Greeks, evoking the function of the one who bears it: to bring good, spiritual profit to others.
G3683.emploi: Onesiphorus appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Paul's second epistle to Timothy. In 2 Timothy 1:16, Paul praises this faithful one for daring to visit him in prison — a courageous act at a time when imprisonment made a Christian suspect — and for having "often comforted" him. In 2 Timothy 4:19, Paul asks Timothy to greet "the family of Onesiphorus," suggesting that Onesiphorus may have disappeared (died, or been absent from Ephesus), but that Paul thinks of his loved ones. These two mentions reveal a man of service and dedication to an apostle in distress.
G3683.portee: Onesiphorus embodies the Christian who dares to show solidarity with a suffering brother, without fear of the world's judgment. His example teaches that true service to the disciples of Christ often involves courage and faithfulness in the shadows: visiting the prisoner, comforting the abandoned, honoring the one publicly renounced. He is a discreet yet fundamental model of Christian love.

sens: large stone used for grinding grain, powered by a donkey
by extension, a heavy and cumbersome object used for crushing
G3684.detail:
1. The word "millstone" refers to the circular stone of a mill — the one that is powered by a donkey to grind grain into flour. It is a massive and very heavy stone, quite different from the small stone used in daily life. Jesus mentions it in Matthew 18:6 and Mark 9:42 as an object so heavy that it crushes everything: to illustrate the terrible punishment awaiting anyone who causes a believing child to stumble.
2. Figuratively, it symbolizes an overwhelming punishment — something inevitable and fatal. The image is that of drowning weighted down by a huge millstone: impossible to rise to the surface, impossible to escape.
G3684.origine: The Greek word comes from "onos" (donkey) with a suffix meaning "belonging to." It literally means "donkey millstone," since only a donkey — or a mule — could move a stone of this size. Jesus specifically chose this word to evoke the largest millstone possible, one that can only be moved by the strength of an animal.
G3684.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament: in Matthew 18:6 and Mark 9:42, where Jesus delivers the same warning in a particularly grave tone. Both texts use exactly this same image of the donkey millstone thrown into the sea as the ultimate punishment. It is a word that Jesus chose for the strength of the image, not for its frequency. It does not appear anywhere else in the Greek New Testament.
G3684.portee: This terrible image from Jesus teaches that causing a child to sin — scandalizing them, turning them away from faith — is a sin of extreme gravity. God does not take it lightly. The Christian reader must draw a serious responsibility from this: to protect the little ones and the weak in faith, and never to be a stumbling block or source of doubt for them.

sens: To derive profit or benefit from something
To enjoy a blessing, a useful help
G3685.detail:
1. The verb expresses the idea of deriving profit or benefit from something, enjoying a concrete advantage. In Philemon 1:20, Paul uses this word in the optative (a wish): he hopes to "gain this advantage from you," meaning to receive from Philemon an act of kindness toward the slave Onesimus who has found favor in Paul's eyes.
2. The meaning extends to the idea of enjoying a blessing, a useful help that benefits the recipient. It is the moral or practical benefit that a generous action provides: Paul desires that Philemon grant him this joy of seeing Onesimus treated with mercy.
G3685.origine: The Greek verb comes from a root expressing the idea of usefulness and personal profit. It is rare in the New Testament and also appears in ancient Greek texts with the meaning of "to benefit from" or "to take advantage of." The word evokes the image of someone receiving something useful that brings them satisfaction.
G3685.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Philemon 1:20. Paul uses it to express his wish — a courteous and affectionate desire — that Philemon "grant him this advantage" in the Lord. The context is that of an intimate letter where Paul intercedes for Onesimus with his master Philemon. The word carries a tone of tenderness here: Paul is not asking for an act of justice, but for an "advantage," a blessing that would bring him joy in the Lord.
G3685.portee: This word reminds the reader that acts of mercy and forgiveness are not experienced as burdensome obligations, but as opportunities for true joy — a joy shared between the giver and the receiver. It is the advantage of a reconciled heart, the profit of grace.

sens: The word by which a person or thing is designated
The entirety of what this word represents: authority, character, reputation, all that implies someone's identity
The authority or power of the one whose name is borne
The person themselves, the individual
G3686.detail:
1. The name is primarily the concrete word given to someone at birth or in an important circumstance. Luke 1:13 reports that the angel said to Zechariah: "You will give him the name John." It is the label, the simplest identification.

2. But in the Bible, the name means much more than that: it expresses all that is known and esteemed about a person, their nature, authority, and reputation. Believing in the "name" of Jesus (John 3:18) does not simply mean believing that his name is Jesus, but believing in who he truly is, in his person and his saving power. Similarly, praying in the "name" of the Lord (James 5:14) means praying with reliance on his authority and power, not just by pronouncing his name.

3. Acting in someone's name means acting with their authority, in their place. The apostles heal and cast out demons "in the name" of Jesus (Acts 3:6): they do not do it by their own power, but by claiming his authority.

4. Rarely, the word simply designates the individual themselves, the person: Acts 1:15 speaks of "one hundred twenty names" present in Jerusalem, meaning one hundred twenty people.
G3686.origine: The Greek word ὄνομα comes from an ancient root meaning "to assign," "to give." In Hebrew, שֵׁם (shem), which it normally translates into Greek, carries the same richness: it is both the word by which someone is called and all that defines them. In the biblical mindset, the name is not just a label, but an extension of the person themselves, charged with meaning and power. The family of related Greek words includes ὀνομάζω (to name), ἐπονομάζω (to give a nickname), etc.
G3686.emploi: The word ὄνομα is extremely frequent in the New Testament, with over 200 occurrences. It is found everywhere: to name the disciples (Matthew 10:2), to report what someone is called (Mark 5:9), to invoke a person (Luke 1:13). In the Gospels, it often involves giving or announcing a name: the birth of Jesus (Matthew 1:21), that of John the Baptist (Luke 1:13). In Acts and the Epistles, the spiritual meaning dominates: believing in the "name" of Jesus (John 1:12, John 3:18), praying in his "name" (John 14:13), suffering for his "name" (Acts 5:41). The word also evokes the glory of God's name that believers must sanctify (Matthew 6:9) and defend against blasphemies. Its significance becomes progressively more theological as one advances through the New Testament.
G3686.portee: For the believer, understanding the biblical weight of the word "name" transforms prayer and the confession of faith. Praying in the name of Jesus is not a magic formula; it is appropriating his authority and intercession. Invoking the name of God touches upon his very character, his attributes, his love. Finally, bearing the name of Christian (1 Peter 4:16) or suffering for the name of Christ is not trivial: it is being identified with him and participating in his destiny.

sens: To give a name to someone or something
To call someone by their name, to designate them
To pronounce someone's name, to invoke them
To be called, to bear a name
G3687.detail:
1. To give a name to someone or something: this is the act of creating or establishing an identity. Jesus "named" Peter (Luke 6:14), meaning He gave him this new name that expressed his new identity and mission. When the twelve apostles are "named" (Mark 3:14, Luke 6:13), they are officially designated and distinguished.
2. To call someone by their name, to designate them: this is to mention someone or something while speaking of them. Paul writes that he wants to preach the Gospel where Christ had not yet been "named" (Romans 15:20), meaning where He had not been spoken of, where His name was not known.
3. To pronounce someone's name, to invoke or use it: this is to invoke someone by pronouncing their name, as when Jewish exorcists try to "invoke" the name of Jesus over the possessed (Acts 19:13).
4. To be called, to bear a name: this is the passive form. Someone who "names" themselves brother but acts badly (1 Corinthians 5:11): they bear the name, the title of brother.
G3687.origine: The word comes from the Greek ὄνομα (onoma), "name." It expresses the action of giving, pronouncing, or bearing a name. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew קָרָא (qara), "to call," and זָכַר (zakar), "to remember" or "to invoke." In the Bible, a name is never just a label: it reveals the true identity and essence of the person.
G3687.emploi: This verb appears 11 times in the New Testament. It primarily describes the action of Jesus choosing and naming His disciples (Mark 3:14, Luke 6:13-14): to name is to recognize and invest. It also means "to mention" or "to speak of": when it is said that Christ had not been named somewhere, it means that He had not been spoken of, that He was not known (Romans 15:20). The verb also expresses the act of invoking a name, as when the name of the Lord is pronounced in exorcism (Acts 19:13). In the passive voice, it means "to be called" or "to call oneself": someone who names themselves brother but lives poorly (1 Corinthians 5:11) bears a title they do not deserve.
G3687.portee: To name someone is to recognize them and give them a place. When Jesus names Peter, He does not merely change his label: He transforms his identity and mission. For the Christian, this word reminds us that our name in Christ has a deep meaning: we are not called by chance. To invoke the name of Jesus is to call Him to our side with the authority of the one who gave it to us and who alone can pronounce it with power.

sens: pack and draft animal, domesticated quadruped
beast of burden used for transport
humble and peaceful animal, symbol of gentleness and service
royal mount in the Old Testament
G3688.detail:
1. The donkey is a domesticated animal of the equine family, smaller and sturdier than a horse, used to carry loads or people. It is an ordinary work animal in the biblical world, accessible to both poor and rich families (Luke 13:15 mentions owners who untie their donkey to water it on the Sabbath).
2. Unlike the horse, a symbol of warrior power, the donkey evokes gentleness, humility, and peaceful service. The prophet Zechariah announced a king who would come riding on a colt (the young of a female donkey), an image taken up in Matthew 21:5 and John 12:15 to describe Jesus' triumphant entry: not as an armed conqueror, but as a humble and gentle king.
3. In the account of Matthew 21:2 and 21:7, the disciples bring a female donkey and her colt, and Jesus sits on them, thus fulfilling this prophecy of royal humility and peace.
G3688.origine: The Greek word ὄνος comes from an ancient root simply designating this animal. In Hebrew, חֲמוֹר (hamor) refers to the male donkey, and אָתוֹן (aton) to the female or she-donkey; the Greek onos can translate either according to the context. The word is attested as early as Homer and similarly designates this humble but indispensable work animal in ancient economy.
G3688.emploi: The word ὄνος appears five times in the Gospels, concentrated in the accounts of Jesus' triumphant entry into Jerusalem (Matthew 21 and John 12) and in a parable in Luke. In Matthew 21:2, Jesus sends His disciples to fetch a female donkey and her colt: He has them untied from a nearby village for Jesus to ride on. In verse 5, Matthew cites the prophecy of Zechariah announcing a king "mounted on a donkey, on a colt." In verse 7, the disciples lay their garments on the female donkey and the colt, and Jesus sits on them. In Luke 13:15, Jesus addresses the Pharisees, calling them "hypocrites," reminding them that each one unties their donkey or ox on the Sabbath to water it; this donkey symbolizes the ordinary and legitimate needs of life. John 12:15 also recalls the messianic prophecy of the king on "the colt of a she-donkey." The meaning remains stable: the humble and peaceful animal, a symbol of service and non-warrior royalty.
G3688.portee: For the believer, the image of Jesus entering Jerusalem on a donkey reveals His messianic identity in an unexpected and profound way: He is king, but not as the world understands it. He does not come as a violent conqueror, but as a prince of peace, humble and accessible. This teaches that true power lies in gentleness and service, not in domination. Jesus' reminder in Luke 13:15 also invites the believer to see beyond rigid religious rules: there is a justice and compassion that transcend the letter, even on the Sabbath.

sens: In a manner consistent with reality, without fiction or appearance
In truth, with assurance and certainty
In an authentic and lasting way
G3689.detail:
1. The word designates what is real, effective, as it truly is and not as it appears. It affirms that something exists or has happened in concrete reality. In Mark 11:32, all "really" held John to be a prophet: this was the sincere conviction of the people, not a mere rumor.
2. The word expresses certainty, the assurance of a truth declared with authority. It is to settle a question, to give a definitive judgment. The centurion in Luke 23:47 says "certainly" this man was just: he is sure, he proclaims it without doubt.
3. The word can qualify what is authentic and lasting, what remains in its deep nature, opposed to what is temporary or superficial. "Really" free in John 8:36 means a true and deep freedom that endures, not an illusory liberation.
G3689.origine: The word comes from the present participle of the verb "to be" (einai in Greek). It literally means "in being," that is, "in the reality of what is." The root thus expresses real existence, concrete being. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it translates words like "amen" (אׇמְנָם) which mean "with certainty" or "in truth."
G3689.emploi: The word appears about ten times in the New Testament, primarily in the Gospels and Pauline epistles. It is always used to affirm a truth against doubt or appearance: John the Baptist was really a prophet (Mark), Christ is really risen (Luke), Christ truly frees (John). Paul uses it to settle doctrinal questions: would justice really come from the law (Galatians)? In the pastoral epistles, it qualifies one who authentically corresponds to their function: a "true" widow (1 Timothy), a "true" life (1 Timothy).
G3689.portee: This word invites the reader to distinguish deceptive appearance from solid reality. For the Christian, it affirms that the resurrection of Christ is not a myth but a real fact, that freedom in Christ is authentic, that God's promises are indeed fulfilled. In the face of the illusions and lies of the world, this word reminds us that only God declares and guarantees what is truly true.

sens: Sour drink made from sour wine
Common beverage of soldiers and poor workers
Image of bitterness and mockery
G3690.detail:
1. Vinegar is sour wine, a cheap and unrefined drink. It is what was called « posca » in the Roman army: soldiers and poor workers drank it to quench their thirst, as it was inexpensive and preserved well. It was carried in skins.

2. At the time of Jesus' crucifixion, soldiers offered him vinegar to drink. In Matthew 27:48, Mark 15:36, and Luke 23:36, they do this in mockery: it is a drink reserved for the lowly, offered to the King. John 19:29 reports the same gesture, but without the explicit intention to mock.

3. Vinegar evokes the bitterness of suffering. In the Old Testament, Psalm 69:21 prophetically announced: « They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink. » By drinking this vinegar, Jesus fulfills this ancient word and fully accepts the bitterness of the Passion.
G3690.origine: The Greek word ὄξος comes from ὀξύς ("sour," "acid"). It literally designates what is acidified. In Hebrew, חֹמֶץ (homets) has the same root and meaning: a sour drink resulting from the fermentation of wine. The Septuagint (Greek translation of the Old Testament) translates this Hebrew word as ὄξος in the passages of Psalm 69:21 and Proverbs 25:20, showing the equivalence between the two words.
G3690.emploi: The word ὄξος appears five times in the New Testament, and all uses concern the crucifixion. Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John all report that vinegar was offered to the crucified Jesus. In Matthew and Mark, this act is clearly a mockery by the soldiers: they offer Jesus the drink of the poor and slaves to ridicule him. John also mentions it, but emphasizes that Jesus "took the vinegar" (John 19:30), which may evoke the voluntary fulfillment of Scripture. The four Gospels agree on this detail, likely seeing it as a realization of the prophecy of Psalm 69:21.
G3690.portee: This humble and painful detail reminds us that Jesus truly suffered in his body and humanity. Offering vinegar to the dying Savior is the ultimate mockery: he is given the drink of the lowest of men. For the believer, this reveals Christ's voluntary humiliation and his solidarity with the suffering. It is also an invitation to recognize his sacrifice as real, bodily, and unvarnished.

sens: Having a sharp edge, capable of cutting
Quick, prompt, agile
G3691.detail:
1. An object that cuts sharply: a sword, a sickle whose edge is sharpened and easily pierces. Revelation speaks several times of the sharp sword coming from the mouth of Christ (Revelation 1:16) or the sharp sickle of the angels (Revelation 14:14, 17, 18): the image evokes a fearsome and effective weapon.

2. What is quick and agile: feet are "light" to move quickly (Romans 3:15), where the psalmist describes those who run swiftly toward evil. The word denotes the liveliness of movement.
G3691.origine: The Greek ὀξύς comes from an Indo-European root suggesting sharpness and point. It is related to Latin words (acutus) and reflects the idea of something sharpened, pointed. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew חַד ("sharp") and קַל ("light, quick"), showing that Greek encompasses both the idea of sharpness and swiftness.
G3691.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in Revelation. It primarily describes weapons: the two-edged sword of Christ (Revelation 1:16 and 2:12), the sickle of the angels at the final judgment (Revelation 14:14, 17, 18 and 19:15). There is only one occurrence in Paul (Romans 3:15) applying the meaning of "quick, light" to the feet of those who shed blood. The apocalyptic use favors the image of sharpness, the edge that divides.
G3691.portee: For the Christian reader, the sharp sword of Christ symbolizes the absolute effectiveness of divine judgment and the Word of God. The sharp sickle of the angels evokes the moment when God harvests: a decisive and precise action. These images remind us that divine intervention is not approximate, but perfectly pointed and irresistible.

sens: Hole or cavity in a wall, ground, or rocky surface
Natural hollow where one can hide or take refuge
Orifice through which a flow comes out (water, speech)
G3692.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a hole or physical opening in something solid: a rock, a mountain, a spring. This is the most concrete image. In Hebrews 11:38, the faithful of the Old Testament hid in the "caves" of the earth — natural cavities that protected them.
2. By extension, it is a hollow, a refuge where one can shelter: a cave, a cavern. The opening then becomes the place of protection and escape from a hostile world.
3. Finally, the word applies to the orifice from which something springs: in James 3:11, the opening is that of the water source, from which both sweet and bitter water spring. The image moves from the hollow to the mouth from which the flow comes.
G3692.origine: The Greek word ὀπή comes from an Indo-European root meaning "to see" or "open." It etymologically designates what is open to view, what is visible — hence: a visible opening, a hole. The word translates in Greek the Hebrew חוֹר (ḥōr, "hole") and חֲגָו (ḥăgāv, "cavity"), terms that are equally concrete and described the refuges of fugitives and the hollows of the earth.
G3692.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, in Hebrews 11:38 and James 3:11 — a rare but precise use. In Hebrews 11, it situates the heroes of faith in the primitive sense: refugees in underground caves, far from comfort, living as fugitives. In James 3, it is used in a comparison: just as a spring cannot pour forth from two different openings — one sweet, the other bitter — so a mouth should not produce both blessing and cursing. The opening thus becomes metaphorically the emblem of what flows from speech.
G3692.portee: This word reminds us that authentic faith often comes at a cost: it requires withdrawing from the world, losing comfort. The faithful of the Old Testament accepted to live hidden in caves rather than deny God. More broadly, the image of the opening in James invites us to monitor what comes out of our mouths: it is an opening from which flows what our heart contains, and we are responsible for that flow.

sens: At the back of a person or thing, on the side of the back
Backwards, following
In the wake of someone, as a disciple or companion
G3693.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning refers to the space located behind someone or something, on the side opposite to the face or front. The woman with a flow of blood approached from behind and touched the edge of Jesus' garment (Luke 8:44), meaning she came to him from the back, remaining out of his sight.
2. The word can also indicate a position behind in space or time, marking a separation or distance. When the disciples say to Jesus, "Send her away, for she is crying out after us" (Matthew 15:23), they mean that she is following them while crying, coming from behind.
3. In a spiritual or metaphorical sense, "behind" can evoke the idea of following or coming after someone. Simon of Cyrene carries the cross behind Jesus (Luke 23:26): he follows him on this painful path. In Revelation, the living creatures also have eyes in the back (Revelation 4:6), suggesting complete vigilance.
G3693.origine: The Greek word ὄπισθεν comes from an Indo-European root related to the idea of "behind" or "back." It primarily corresponds to the Hebrew words אָחוֹר (ahor, "back") and אַחַר (ahar, "after"), which share the same spatial and temporal intuition. The French preposition "derrière" and this Greek word carry the same fundamental image: what is at the back, out of direct sight.
G3693.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Synoptic Gospels and Revelation. In the Gospels, it first describes a physical approach: the woman with a flow of blood approaches Jesus from behind (Matthew 9:20, Mark 5:27, Luke 8:44), a detail that emphasizes her discretion and humility. The word is also used to express a position of following or discipleship: Simon carries the cross behind Jesus (Luke 23:26), and the disciples are addressed by a woman who cries out behind them (Matthew 15:23). In Revelation (4:6, 5:1), the term takes on a more cosmic significance, describing the eyes of the living creatures that look both behind and in front, symbolizing an omnidirectional or divine perception.
G3693.portee: This word reminds us that a humble and discreet approach finds grace with Jesus. The woman who touches his garment from behind, without seeking attention, is healed and recognized. It invites us to meditate on what it means to "follow" Jesus: not to be in the foreground, but to accept walking behind him, like Simon carrying his cross. It is a lesson on humility and authentic discipleship.

sens: Behind someone or something in space
Following someone, in their wake
Subsequently to an event in time
In the back, what is past or gone
Figuratively: placing oneself under the authority or example of someone
G3694.detail:
1. The literal spatial sense: "after" designates what is behind, in the back. When Jesus says in Luke 24:18, "do not turn back to take his cloak," he is speaking of a physical movement backward. It is the simple idea of position behind.

2. Following someone: "after" can mean "in the wake of," walking behind a person. When Jesus calls his disciples in Mark 1:17 with "Come after me," he invites them to follow him physically, then spiritually. This already shifts from the spatial to the relational.

3. The order in time: "after" indicates that one event comes subsequent to another. John 1:30 expresses it this way: "After me comes a man," meaning someone who arrives after John the Baptist chronologically. Time is ordered forward and backward.

4. The past: the expression "what is behind" (Philippians 3:13) speaks of everything one leaves behind — memories, guilt, past achievements that should not be dwelled upon.

5. Imitation or adherence: in Mark 8:34, "come after me" does not only mean to walk behind Jesus, but to adhere to his cause, live according to his principles, become his disciple. It is a spiritual commitment expressed through a spatial image.
G3694.origine: The word comes from an ancient Greek root expressing the back, the background. In classical Greek, "opisō" is both an adverb and a preposition, marking the position behind in space or the order of succession. In the Greek Bible (Septuagint), it regularly translates the Hebrew word "achar" (אַחַר), which carries the same two meanings: first spatial ("back"), then temporal ("after"). This dual dimension, spatial first, temporal next, is characteristic of ancient languages, which conceive of time as a direction in space.
G3694.emploi: The word appears 36 times in the New Testament, mainly in Matthew, Mark, and Luke. It functions as an adverb ("behind," "back," "after") or as a preposition governing a genitive ("after someone"). Its uses vary: temporal in Matthew 3:11 ("he who comes after me"), spatial in Luke 7:38 (the sinful woman places herself behind Jesus), spiritual in Mark 8:34 ("come after me" means to be a disciple). The expression "what is behind" (Philippians 3:13) is a fixed usage, almost nominalized. The uses with the verb "follow" show how "after" and "follow" complement each other: the first is more spatial and directional, the second more volitional. In Revelation, notably 13:3, "to follow him" (literally "to go after") expresses adherence to a false authority, which shows the religious power of the term.
G3694.portee: This word reveals how Christian faith in the New Testament is conceived in terms of movement: one does not adhere to Jesus through abstract doctrine, but by "following" him, going "after" him. It is incarnate, concrete. This invites the reader not to remain fixated on what is "behind" (their sins, past failures) but to orient their gaze and steps toward what is ahead — the future in God. The verb "to follow" thus becomes an existential call: to be a Christian is to walk in the direction of Christ, not just to profess a belief.

sens: To equip someone with combat weapons
To prepare to fight by taking up arms
To strengthen mentally or morally to face a trial
G3695.detail:
1. In the literal sense, it is to equip a soldier with weapons for battle. The Greek word ὁπλίζω comes from ὅπλον ("weapon"), and it designates the concrete action of preparing a warrior for battle by providing him with military equipment.

2. In the reflexive form ("to arm oneself"), the soldier himself takes up arms and prepares for combat. It is the action of seizing one's weapons to defend or attack.

3. Figuratively, "to arm" means to fortify someone morally or spiritually so that they can face a difficult trial. In 1 Peter 4:1, Peter exhorts Christians to "arm yourselves with the same mindset" as Christ — that is, to mentally clothe themselves with his resolve and conviction, just as one puts on armor before battle.
G3695.origine: The Greek word ὁπλίζω derives from ὅπλον, which means "weapon" or "military equipment." The image is that of the warrior preparing by donning his arms. This root also recalls the French "hoplites" (heavily armed soldiers of ancient Greece). In Hebrew, the corresponding concept is often expressed by verbs meaning "to gird" or "to equip."
G3695.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 4:1, in the reflexive form: "arm yourselves with the same mindset." Peter uses it in a context of spiritual encouragement in the face of suffering. Readers are called to mentally don the disposition of Christ in the face of suffering, as one puts on armor. This unique usage shows how the New Testament transposes the concrete military language of combat into the moral and spiritual realm: the true strength of the Christian lies in their unwavering conviction, not in material weapons.
G3695.portee: This verse invites the Christian to strengthen their faith and courage in the face of trials by imitating Christ's resolve. The image of spiritual arming teaches that the Christian life is a battle where one must prepare mentally and morally, adopting the mindset and resolve of Christ. It is a call not to remain passive in the face of suffering, but to internally equip oneself with conviction and strength.

sens: Tool or instrument used to accomplish a task
Weapon of war, sword, spear, or other combat equipment
Figuratively: means or moral power used to fight against evil or sin
G3696.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to any tool or instrument used for an action. In Romans 6:13, our "members" (hands, eyes, mouth) can become instruments for sin or for righteousness — just as one uses a weapon.
2. Literally, a weapon of war: sword, spear, shield. John 18:3 mentions the soldiers who came to arrest Jesus with "weapons" for physical combat.
3. The Bible uses this word in a moral and spiritual sense: our actions, our words, our steadfastness become "weapons" to fight against sin, doubt, and evil. Romans 13:12 speaks of the "weapons of light" to put on as armor, and 2 Corinthians 10:4 asserts that our spiritual "weapons" (prayer, faith, truth) are more powerful than those of the flesh.
G3696.origine: The Greek word ὅπλον comes from the ancient military domain. It originally refers to the equipment of the hoplite soldier. The Bible uses it by analogy: just as a sword is used to fight a physical enemy, righteousness, truth, and the word of God are used to fight spiritually. This image of combat and armament is central to the teaching of the New Testament.
G3696.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament, almost always in the plural ("weapons"). John 18:3 uses it in a concrete sense: the soldiers come with "weapons" to arrest Jesus. But Paul systematically uses it in a figurative sense when speaking of our spiritual struggle. In Romans 6:13, our members are "instruments" — the same Greek word — that can serve evil or good. In Romans 13:12 and 2 Corinthians 6:7 and 10:4, the "weapons" become spiritual realities: light, righteousness, truth. The passage in 2 Corinthians 10:4 is the most explicit: our "weapons" are not carnal, but spiritual and divine.
G3696.portee: This word reminds Christians that their daily life is a form of spiritual combat. Our choices, our words, our behavior are never neutral: they place us on the side of righteousness or sin. Understanding that our body and will are "weapons" calls us to consciously place them in the service of God and not of evil. It is an invitation to not live passively, but to actively fight against sin by the power of God.

sens: of what kind, of what nature
what kind of
how (interrogative or narrative)
G3697.detail: 1. The word poses a question about the kind, category, or quality of something: "what is this object?", "of what nature is this work?" It is the inquiry about type or quality. In 1 Corinthians 3:13, Paul asks that the fire test "what each one's work is" — that is, its nature, whether it is solid or fragile. 2. It can also express a comparative link: "such as", "in such a way that". In Acts 26:29, Paul wishes that his listeners become "such as I am" — not exactly like him, but of the same spiritual type, freed from idols as he is. 3. In a narrative context, it indirectly reports a question about quality or appearance: "what he was like" (James 1:24) simply means his aspect, what one sees when looking at him.
G3697.origine: The Greek word ὁποῖος (hopoios) is formed from ὅ-ποι-ος, literally "who of what type". It combines an interrogative particle (ὁ- or ὅ-, equivalent to the French "which") with an element that denotes kind or type. It is both an interrogative and a relative word: it can pose a direct question ("which?") or express an indirect relationship ("in such a way that"). It belongs to the large family of Greek interrogative adjectives and is related to other forms like τίς (tis, "who?") but specialized in questioning quality rather than identity.
G3697.emploi: This word appears 5 times in the New Testament, always to inquire or designate the nature, kind, or quality of something. In 1 Corinthians 3:13, it questions the nature of each one's spiritual work — how the fire will reveal its true substance. In Galatians 2:6, it indirectly reports the question: it does not matter "what they were" these great apostles — their past rank changes nothing for Paul. In 1 Thessalonians 1:9, it speaks of "what access" Paul and his companions had, meaning what kind of reception, what sort of relationship. In James 1:24, the man forgets "what he was like" when looking at himself in the mirror — forgets his own appearance. In Acts 26:29, Paul wishes that the listeners become "such as I am" — a comparison of nature or state. Thus, the word serves to inquire, compare, or indirectly report on the qualities of beings and things.
G3697.portee: This word reminds us of the importance of the true nature of things rather than appearances. By asking "which", Paul invites the reader to examine the quality of their spiritual work, not to be impressed by the rank or outward appearance of people, and not to forget who they truly are in Christ. It is an invitation to sincerity and depth in the Christian life.

sens: In a place, at what location
To what place, in what direction (with a verb of movement)
In the circumstances where, in the condition that
By the reason that, since
G3699.detail:
1. The most common and straightforward meaning: the word designates the place where something is or happens. "Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy" (Matthew 6:19) — it refers to the earthly place where riches corrupt. It introduces a relative clause that specifies the location: "Another seed fell on rocky ground, where it did not have much soil" (Mark 4:5).
2. With a verb of movement (to go, to come, to follow), the word takes on the meaning of "to where", "in what direction": "You cannot follow me now where I am going, but you will follow me later" (John 13:36) means "to the place where I am going", towards the destiny that Jesus is heading.
3. In certain contexts, it expresses a condition or circumstance rather than a strict location: "Where there is neither Greek nor Jew" (Colossians 3:11) means "in the condition where" or "among those in whom".
4. Rarely, it introduces a cause or reason: "Because you are carnal" (1 Corinthians 3:3) — the word marks here why the Corinthians are jealous and quarrelsome.
G3699.origine: The Greek word « hopou » comes from the root « ho » (the, that one) combined with « pou » (where). It is a relative adverb of place, related to the interrogative word « ποῦ » (pou, where?). It often corresponds to the Hebrew « šām » (there) or « ašer » (who, that) when the Greek Old Testament translates Hebrew texts. The word primarily expresses a concrete location before extending to more abstract meanings.
G3699.emploi: The word "where" is extremely frequent in the New Testament (78 occurrences). It appears in all the Gospels and in the Epistles. Its use varies according to context: in parables and narratives, it localizes the action ("where there was a synagogue"), in Jesus' teachings, it takes on a spiritual significance ("where two or three are gathered in my name"). With verbs of movement, it designates less the static place than the direction or destination ("where you go", "where I am"). In the Epistles, it can also mark a condition or state: "where there is neither slave nor free" (Galatians 3:28 implicit) speaks of the Christian community. The meaning generally remains clear: it is about situating in space or, by extension, in a spiritual reality.
G3699.portee: Recognizing the role of this small word helps to follow the movement of narratives and the logic of teaching. When Jesus speaks of treasures "where moth and rust destroy", he invites us to see the contrast between what perishes and what remains. When he says "where I am, there will my servant be also", the word "where" is no longer a simple geographical address, but a promise of presence and destiny: to follow Jesus is to go where he goes, to enter into his world of resurrection.
